A claim circulating on social media asserts that if a person can hold their breath from point A to point B—a test lasting between 20 to 24 seconds—they can be free from COVID-19. This breath-holding challenge, often shared in videos and posts, suggests that successfully completing the test indicates a lack of COVID-19 infection. The claim has gained traction during the pandemic, leading many to believe in its validity as a simple self-diagnostic tool.

To understand the origins and implications of this claim, it is important to recall the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic. At the time, widespread uncertainty and fear prompted numerous unofficial remedies and self-diagnosis methods to appear online. One such method was the “breath-holding test,” which purportedly allowed individuals to rule out COVID-19 infection if they could hold their breath for a certain duration without coughing, discomfort, or other symptoms.

The reasoning behind the claim is based on a misunderstanding of how COVID-19 affects the lungs and respiratory system. COVID-19, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, can infect people with a wide range of symptoms—including no symptoms at all in some cases. While the virus can cause respiratory distress and, in severe cases, pneumonia or reduced lung function, these symptoms do not always appear in the early stages of infection. Many people with COVID-19 experience mild symptoms or are entirely asymptomatic, especially in the initial days after exposure. Therefore, the ability to hold one’s breath for 20 to 24 seconds does not reliably indicate the absence of infection.

Medical professionals and public health authorities have consistently warned against relying on self-administered breath-holding tests as a diagnostic tool for COVID-19. There is no scientific basis for the idea that such a test can confirm or rule out infection. Breath-holding capacity varies widely between individuals and can be influenced by a variety of factors unrelated to COVID-19, such as age, fitness level, underlying health conditions, anxiety, or even how deeply a person inhales before the test.

Moreover, some individuals with COVID-19 may retain normal lung function, especially in the early stages, and would easily pass the breath-holding test, while others with unrelated respiratory or anxiety issues might fail the test despite not having the virus. This could lead to false reassurance or unnecessary worry.

The only reliable ways to determine if someone has COVID-19 are through approved diagnostic tests, such as PCR or rapid antigen tests, conducted by medical professionals or authorized testing centers. Preventive measures—such as vaccination, mask-wearing, hand hygiene, and social distancing—remain the best ways to protect against the virus.

In summary, the breath-holding test circulating on social media as a way to self-diagnose COVID-19 is not supported by scientific evidence and should not be used as a substitute for proper testing or medical advice. Relying on such misinformation can be dangerous, as it may delay proper diagnosis and treatment or contribute to the spread of the virus.

Ujian nahan napas iki, sering dibagikan di video maupun postingan, ngandika yen berhasil melakonan ujian iki bisa menunjukkan kekurangan infeksi virus korona. Ajan iki diterima luas selama pandemi, ngajak banyak orang percaya kualitasnya sebaga alat diagnostik mandiri.

Untuk ngertos asal-usul maupun implikasi ajan iki, penting untuk mengingat masa awal pandemi virus korona. Saat itu, ketidakpastian dan ketakutan yang meluas mendorong munculnya berbagai cara pengobatan tidak resmi maupun metode diagnostik mandiri di internet. Salah satunya iku "ujian nahan napas", ngandika yen seseorang bisa menolak infeksi virus korona kalo bisa nahan napas selama waktu tertentu tanpa batuk, ketidaknyamanan, maupun gejala lain.

Alasan di balik ajan iki didasarkan pada pemahaman yang salah tentang bagaimana virus korona mempengaruhi paru-paru maupun sistem pernapasan. Virus korona, disebabkan oleh virus SARS-CoV-2, bisa menyerang manusia dengan berbagai gejala—termasuk tanpa gejala sama sekali pada beberapa kasus. Banyak orang yang terinfeksi virus korona mengalami gejala ringan atau sama sekali tidak mengalami gejala, terutama di hari-hari awal setelah terpapar. Oleh karena itu, kemampuan untuk nahan napas selama 20 sampai 24 detik tidak secara andal menunjukkan ketiadaan infeksi.

Ahli medis maupun otoritas kesehatan masyarakat konsisten memperingatkan jangan mengandalkan ujian nahan napas mandiri sebagai alat diagnostik untuk virus korona. Tidak ada dasar ilmiah untuk gagasan bahwa ujian semacam ini bisa mengonfirmasi atau menolak infeksi. Kemampuan nahan napas bervariasi antar individu dan bisa dipengaruhi oleh berbagai faktor yang tidak terkait dengan virus korona, seperti usia, tingkat kebugaran, kondisi kesehatan dasar, kecemasan, maupun seberapa dalam seseorang menghirup sebelum ujian.

Selain itu, beberapa orang yang terinfeksi virus korona mungkin tetap memiliki fungsi paru-paru normal, terutama di tahap awal infeksi, dan akan dengan mudah lulus ujian nahan napas, sementara orang lain yang mengalami masalah pernapasan atau kecemasan yang tidak terkait virus korona mungkin gagal dalam ujian meskipun tidak terinfeksi. Hal ini bisa menyebabkan rasa aman yang salah atau kekhawatiran yang tidak perlu.

Cara yang paling andal untuk menentukan apakah seseorang terinfeksi virus korona adalah melalui tes diagnostik yang disetujui, seperti tes PCR atau tes antigen cepat, yang dilakukan oleh tenaga medis maupun pusat pengujian yang berwenang. Upaya pencegahan—seperti vaksinasi, memakai masker, kebersihan tangan, maupun jarak sosial—tetap menjadi cara terbaik untuk melindungi diri dari virus ini.

Secara keseluruhan, ujian nahan napas yang beredar di media sosial sebagai cara mandiri untuk mendiagnosis virus korona tidak didukung oleh bukti ilmiah dan seharusnya tidak digunakan sebagai pengganti tes yang tepat maupun nasihat medis. Mengandalkan informasi yang salah bisa berbahaya, karena bisa menghambat diagnosis maupun pengobatan yang tepat atau berkontribusi pada penyebaran virus.

A social media post claims that the traditional Chinese medicine formula NRICM101 can help cure COVID-19 and, furthermore, can protect and maintain health even for those not infected with the virus. The assertion taps into widespread interest in alternative treatments and preventive measures during the COVID-19 pandemic. This article examines the claim by reviewing the background of NRICM101, its application, and available evidence regarding its efficacy and safety.

NRICM101 is a herbal formula developed in Taiwan during the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic. It is composed of several herbs traditionally used in Chinese medicine and was designed with the intent to address symptoms and progression of viral respiratory infections. NRICM101 has been used in some hospitals within Taiwan as part of an adjunct therapy for COVID-19 patients, particularly those with mild or moderate symptoms.

The core claim in the social media post is twofold: first, that NRICM101 can help cure COVID-19, and second, that it can protect and maintain overall health even in the absence of infection. It is important to note that, as of now, there is no universally recognized cure for COVID-19; instead, treatments focus on symptom management, supporting recovery, and reducing the risk of complications. Standard protocols worldwide include antiviral medications, supportive therapies, and, in severe cases, hospitalization and intensive care.

Evidence related to NRICM101’s effectiveness against COVID-19 is limited and primarily comes from small-scale studies and observational reports. Some research from Taiwan has suggested that patients receiving NRICM101 alongside standard care experienced shorter hospital stays and improved symptom relief compared to those receiving standard care alone. However, these studies often lack rigorous controls, large sample sizes, and peer-reviewed validation. International health agencies have not officially recommended NRICM101 as a treatment for COVID-19, and it is not included in global COVID-19 treatment guidelines.

The second part of the claim—that NRICM101 can protect and maintain health for uninfected individuals—is even less substantiated by scientific evidence. While traditional Chinese medicine often emphasizes preventive health and holistic well-being, there is currently no clinical proof that NRICM101 can prevent COVID-19 infection or confer general health benefits to healthy individuals. The safety profile of NRICM101 for long-term use in healthy populations remains unclear.

It is crucial for consumers to be cautious with health claims regarding COVID-19 treatments. The best protection against COVID-19 remains vaccination, masking, and adherence to public health guidelines. While NRICM101 may have a role as a complementary therapy in certain regulated settings, it should not be considered a cure or a substitute for established preventive measures. Individuals interested in using herbal supplements should consult qualified healthcare professionals before starting any new treatment, particularly for serious illnesses like COVID-19.

In summary, current evidence does not support the claim that NRICM101 can cure COVID-19 or provide health protection for uninfected individuals. The formula may be used as an adjunct in some cases, but its effects are not conclusively proven, and it should not replace standard medical care or preventive practices.

Claims circulating on social media allege that Pastor Huang of the River of Life Christian Church died following his COVID-19 vaccination, and that more than 20 Chinese individuals have developed myocarditis after receiving COVID-19 vaccine shots. These statements have raised concerns about vaccine safety, particularly within faith-based and Chinese communities. This article examines the veracity of these claims, drawing on available evidence and broader context regarding COVID-19 vaccines and myocarditis.

**Background on COVID-19 Vaccines and Myocarditis**

Since the rollout of COVID-19 vaccines worldwide, questions about their safety have been frequently raised. Myocarditis, an inflammation of the heart muscle, has been recognized as a rare but documented side effect associated with some mRNA COVID-19 vaccines, particularly among young males. However, health authorities globally emphasize that such cases are uncommon and that the benefits of vaccination in preventing severe COVID-19 illness outweigh the risks of rare adverse events.

**Investigating the Claim about Pastor Huang**

The post specifically claims that Pastor Huang of the River of Life Christian Church died after receiving a COVID-19 vaccine. River of Life Christian Church is an established congregation with a significant following, particularly among Chinese-speaking communities. Following this claim, no verifiable reports from credible news outlets or official church statements have substantiated that Pastor Huang’s death was directly caused by a COVID-19 vaccine. In fact, in most documented cases of post-vaccination deaths, thorough medical investigations are conducted to establish causality, as temporal association does not equate to causation.

Without official medical records or a public statement from the church or the family linking Pastor Huang’s death to the vaccine, this claim remains unsubstantiated. It is important to note that millions of people have been vaccinated, and deaths unrelated to vaccination can occur coincidentally after immunization due to other health conditions.

**Examining the Myocarditis Claim**

The post also asserts that more than 20 Chinese individuals experienced myocarditis after receiving COVID-19 vaccinations. While there have been isolated reports of myocarditis following vaccination, especially among younger people, these cases are rare relative to the number of doses administered. Health authorities in China and worldwide monitor vaccine side effects through surveillance systems. Most cases of vaccine-associated myocarditis have been mild, with patients recovering fully.

It is also important to consider that COVID-19 infection itself carries a higher risk of myocarditis compared to vaccination. The risk-benefit analysis conducted by global health agencies consistently finds that the protective effects of vaccination outweigh these rare risks.

**Conclusion**

While the concerns raised in the post warrant careful consideration, current evidence does not support the claim that Pastor Huang’s death was caused by a COVID-19 vaccine. The assertion that more than 20 Chinese individuals suffered myocarditis after vaccination is plausible in the context of rare side effects; however, such cases are extremely uncommon and typically not severe. The overall scientific consensus remains that COVID-19 vaccines are safe and effective for the vast majority of people. Public discussion about vaccine safety should be grounded in verified information and guided by medical expertise.

The social media post claims that a Covid patient with a cycle threshold (CT) value of 12 is much more infectious than one with a CT value of 30. This assertion centers on the use of CT values from PCR (polymerase chain reaction) tests, which are widely used to detect SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for Covid-19. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to understand what CT values represent, how they are interpreted, and their relevance to infectiousness.

PCR testing works by amplifying genetic material from a virus in cycles. The cycle threshold (CT) value is the number of amplification cycles required to detect viral RNA in a sample. A lower CT value means that fewer cycles were needed to detect the virus, indicating a higher amount of viral genetic material in the sample. Conversely, a higher CT value means that more cycles were required, suggesting a lower amount of viral RNA is present.

Generally, CT values can range from below 15 to above 40, depending on the test and laboratory protocols. In clinical interpretation, a CT value of 12 indicates a very high viral load, while a CT value of 30 suggests a much lower viral load. The infectiousness of a patient is often correlated with viral load: higher viral loads are typically associated with greater potential to transmit the virus to others.

Research and real-world observations have shown that people with lower CT values (e.g., 12) are more likely to shed viable virus, meaning they can more easily infect others via respiratory droplets or surfaces. In contrast, individuals with higher CT values (e.g., 30) often have lower or even non-detectable levels of infectious virus, particularly as they recover from Covid-19 or are late in the course of infection. Some laboratories and health authorities use CT cutoffs to help guide isolation and return-to-work policies, with the understanding that higher CT values may indicate reduced infectiousness.

However, it is important to note that CT values can be influenced by several factors beyond viral load. These include the type of sample collected, the time since infection onset, the specific PCR assay used, and laboratory procedures. CT values are not standardized across all testing platforms, which means that direct comparison between tests or individuals can be unreliable. Additionally, CT values alone should not be used to make definitive decisions about a patient's infectiousness; clinical context, symptoms, and other findings are also important.

In summary, the core claim that a Covid patient with a CT value of 12 is much more infectious than one with a CT value of 30 is generally accurate when interpreting CT values as an indirect measure of viral load. Lower CT values correspond to higher viral loads and a greater likelihood of transmitting the virus. However, clinical interpretation of CT values requires caution due to variability in testing methods and individual circumstances. While CT values are a useful tool in assessing infectiousness, they should be considered alongside other clinical and epidemiological information.

Šī apgalvojuma pamatā ir CT vērtības izmantošana PCR (polimerāzēšanas ķēdes reakcija) testos, kas plaši izmantoti SARS-CoV-2 vīrusa (Covid-19 izraisītāja) detekcijai. Lai novērtētu šīs apgalvojuma precizitāti, svarīgi ir saprast, kas ir CT vērtības, kā tās tulkot, un kā tās saistītas ar inficējamišķību.

PCR testa darbība balstās uz genetiskā materiāla amplifikāciju ciklos. Ciklu slēguma (CT) vērtība ir ciklu skaits, kas nepieciešams, lai identificētu vīrusa RNA paraugā. Zema CT vērtība nozīmē, ka vīrusu identificēja ar mazāk ciklu, kas norāda uz augstu vīrusa genetiskā materiāla daudzumu paraugā. Pretēji, augsta CT vērtība nozīmē, ka vajadzēja vairāk ciklu, kas norāda uz zemāku vīrusa RNA daudzumu.

Kopumā CT vērtības var svārstīties no zemāk par 15 līdz augstāk par 40, atkarībā no testa un laboratorijas protokolu. Kliniskā interpretācijā CT vērtība 12 norāda uz ļoti augstu vīrusa lodi, savukārt CT vērtība 30 norāda uz zemāku vīrusa lodēm. Pacienta inficējamišķība bieži ir saistīta ar vīrusa lodēm: augstākas vīrusa lodes parasti ir saistītas ar lielāku iespēju inficēt citus cilvēkus.

Pētījumi un reālās observācijas parādījušas, ka cilvēki ar zemākiem CT vērtībām (piemēram, 12) ir vairāk iespējami, lai izdalītu dzīvu vīrusu, tādējādi varot vieglāk inficēt citus cilvēkus ar elpošanas dzidru vai virsmām. Pretēji, cilvēki ar augstākiem CT vērtībām (piemēram, 30) dažreiz ir zemākas vai pat neizmērojamas inficējamas vīrusa lodes, īpaši, kad tie atveseļojas no koronavīrusa infekcijas vai ir vēlā stadijā. Daži laboratorijas un veselības aģentūras izmanto CT slieksni, lai palīdzētu vadīt izolācijas un atgriešanās darbā politikas, saprazdami, ka augstākas CT vērtības var norādīt uz mazāku inficējamišķību.

Tomēr svarīgi atzīt, ka CT vērtības var būt ietekmētas vairākiem faktoriem, kas nav tikai vīrusa lode. Šie faktori ietver parauga veidu, infekcijas sākuma laikposmu, izmantoto konkrēto PCR testu un laboratorijas procedūras. CT vērtības nav standartizētas visās testēšanas platformās, kas nozīmē, ka tieša salīdzinājuma starp testiem vai indivīdiem var būt nepārtraukta. Papildus, CT vērtības patiess nevar izmantot, lai pieņemtu noteiktus lēmumus par pacienta inficējamišķību; kliniskā konteksts, simptomi un citas atklājumi arī ir svarīgi.

Kopumā, galvenais apgalvojums, ka koronavīrusa pacients ar CT vērtību 12 ir daudz vairāk inficējams nekā pacients ar CT vērtību 30, bieži ir precīzs, interpretējot CT vērtības kā neposmīgu vīrusa lodes mēru. Zemākas CT vērtības atbilst augstākai vīrusa lodēm un lielākai iespējai pārnesēt vīrusu. Tomēr CT vērtību kliniskā interpretācija prasa uzmanību, jo testēšanas metodes un individuālās apstākļi var mainīties. Kaunīgi, CT vērtības ir noderīga rīkā, lai novērtētu inficējamišķību, tām jābūt izmantotām kopā ar citām kliniskām un epidemioloģiskām informācijām.

A viral video circulating on social media claims to show Indian people vandalizing religious idols in temples, allegedly because these idols did not “bless them” during the COVID-19 pandemic. The video has sparked debate and concern online, as viewers question its authenticity and the broader implications it suggests about religious sentiment in India during a time of crisis. This article examines the claim, provides context, and analyzes the evidence available.

Context and Background

India is a diverse nation with deep religious roots, and idol worship is a core practice in many faith traditions, particularly Hinduism. Temples and shrines are central to community life, and idols representing gods and goddesses are venerated as embodiments of divine power. During the COVID-19 pandemic, which hit India hard and led to significant loss of life and economic hardship, many people turned to spiritual practices for comfort and hope.

However, the pandemic also led to widespread frustration, fear, and questioning of established norms, including religious rituals. In some cases, news outlets reported isolated incidents of people expressing anger at religious institutions, questioning why prayers and rituals did not deliver relief from the pandemic’s effects. Such sentiments, while rare and not representative of the broader population, have occasionally surfaced during times of crisis.

Analysis of the Video and Fact-Checking the Claim

The claim at hand asserts that Indian people vandalized idols because they felt these idols failed to protect them during the pandemic. To assess its accuracy, it’s necessary to review the video itself and understand its origins.

In many instances, videos shared on social media lack proper context. Clips may be edited, miscaptioned, or taken out of context to create a misleading narrative. Upon close examination, some videos purportedly showing idol vandalism have been traced to unrelated events, such as disputes over temple management, local grievances, or acts of theft. In several cases, authorities have clarified that vandalism was not motivated by pandemic-related disappointment, but stemmed from other causes, including property disputes or criminal intent.

There have been isolated reports in India of individuals expressing anger toward religious icons during the pandemic, but these incidents are extremely rare and not indicative of widespread sentiment. Moreover, the idea that people en masse vandalized idols because they felt “unblessed” during COVID-19 is not supported by credible reports from law enforcement or major news organizations. Religious faith remains strong for the vast majority of Indians, and most communities continued traditional worship, either in-person when permitted, or virtually.

Conclusion

While it is true that the pandemic led to questions and frustrations regarding faith and spiritual practices, the claim that Indian people broadly vandalized idols because they were not blessed during the pandemic is misleading. Isolated incidents may exist, but there is no evidence to support the assertion of widespread or systematic idol vandalism motivated by such disappointment. The video circulating online lacks clear context, and viewers should be cautious about drawing conclusions based on incomplete or potentially manipulated footage. As always, verifying the source and context of viral content is essential before accepting its claims at face value.

Artikel ini mengulas klaim tersebut, memberikan konteks, dan menganalisis bukti yang tersedia.

Konteks dan Latar Belakang

India adolah negara yang beragam denga akar agama yang dalam, dan pengagungan patung adolah praktik inti di banyak tradisi kepercayaan, khususnya Hinduisme. Pura dan kuil adolah pusat kehidupan komunitas, dan patung-patung yang mewakili dewa dan dewi dihormati sebagai wujud kekuatan ilahi. Selama pandemi COVID-19, yang sangat menghancurkan India dan menyebabkan kerugian besar dalam nyawa dan kesulitan ekonomi, banyak orang beralih ke praktik spiritual untuk mencari ketenangan dan harapan.

Namun, pandemi juga menyebabkan kekecewaan, ketakutan, dan pertanyaan terhadap norma-norma yang telah lama berlaku, termasuk ritual agama. Dalam beberapa kasus, media melaporkan insiden terisolasi di mana orang menunjukkan kemarahan terhadap institusi agama, mempertanyakan mengapa doa dan ritual tidak memberikan perlindungan dari efek pandemi. Perasaan semacam ini, meskipun langka dan tidak mewakili mayoritas populasi, secara terpisah telah muncul pada masa krisis.

Analisis Video dan Pemeriksaan Fakta Klaim

Klaim yang dibahas menunjukkan bahwa warga India menghancurkan patung karena mereka merasa patung-patung tersebut tidak melindungi mereka selama pandemi. Untuk mengevaluasi keakuratan klaim ini, perlu melihat video itu sendiri dan memahami asal-usulnya.

Dalam banyak kasus, video yang dibagikan di media sosial kurang memiliki konteks yang tepat. Potongan video bisa diedit, disalahcaption, atau diambil dari konteks yang berbeda untuk menciptakan narasi yang salah. Setelah diperiksa secara mendalam, beberapa video yang diduga menunjukkan penghancuran patung ternyata berasal dari kejadian yang tidak terkait, seperti perselisihan tentang pengelolaan pura, keluhan lokal, atau tindakan pencurian. Dalam beberapa kasus, otoritas telah menjelaskan bahwa penghancuran tidak disebabkan oleh kekecewaan terhadap pandemi, melainkan karena penyebab lain, termasuk perselisihan kepemilikan atau niat kriminal.

Ada laporan terisolasi di India tentang individu yang menunjukkan kemarahan terhadap ikon agama selama pandemi, tetapi insiden-insiden ini sangat langka dan tidak mencerminkan sentimen yang luas. Lebih lanjut, gagasan bahwa orang-orang secara massal menghancurkan patung karena merasa "tidak diberkati" selama pandemi COVID-19 tidak didukung oleh laporan yang dapat dipercaya dari lembaga penegak hukum atau organisasi berita utama. Kepercayaan agama tetap kuat bagi kebanyakan warga India, dan kebanyakan komunitas terus melaksanakan ibadah tradisional, baik secara langsung ketika diizinkan, maupun secara virtual.

Kesimpulan

Meskipun benar bahwa pandemi menyebabkan pertanyaan dan kekecewaan terhadap iman dan praktik spiritual, klaim bahwa warga India secara luas menghancurkan patung karena mereka tidak diberkati selama pandemi adalah salah. Insiden terisolasi mungkin ada, tetapi tidak ada bukti yang mendukung klaim tentang penghancuran patung secara luas atau sistematis yang disebabkan oleh kekecewaan semacam itu. Video yang beredar di internet kurang memiliki konteks yang jelas, dan penonton sebaiknya berhati-hati dalam menarik kesimpulan berdasarkan footage yang tidak lengkap atau potensi dimanipulasi. Seperti selalu, memverifikasi sumber dan konteks konten viral sangat penting sebelum menerima klaimnya secara langsung.

article_content:
A social media post has recently gained attention for claiming that drinking NRICM101, a traditional Chinese medicine, every day can cure COVID-19 or prevent infection. Such statements about medical treatments and preventive measures require careful scrutiny, especially concerning a disease as serious and globally impactful as COVID-19.

NRICM101 is a herbal formula developed in Taiwan and promoted as a traditional remedy for respiratory illnesses. Its formulation includes several herbs commonly used in traditional Chinese medicine and was initially intended to address symptoms associated with COVID-19. During the early stages of the pandemic, some hospitals in Asia incorporated NRICM101 as a complementary therapy alongside standard COVID-19 treatments. Its use was primarily focused on symptom relief and potential support for recovery, not as a standalone cure or preventive measure.

To assess the claim’s validity, it is crucial to understand how COVID-19 is treated and prevented according to current scientific consensus. COVID-19 is caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, and approved treatments include antiviral medications, supportive care, and—when appropriate—hospital interventions such as oxygen therapy. Prevention strategies center on vaccination, mask-wearing, hand hygiene, and physical distancing. While some alternative and traditional therapies have been studied for their potential supportive effects, none have been universally recognized as cures or sole preventive agents.

Regarding NRICM101, available studies suggest it may have anti-inflammatory and antiviral properties and could help alleviate symptoms in mild cases of COVID-19. However, these findings are preliminary and based on limited clinical data. No large-scale, peer-reviewed studies have demonstrated that NRICM101 can cure COVID-19 or reliably prevent infection. Regulatory authorities and mainstream medical organizations have not endorsed NRICM101 as a substitute for vaccination or approved therapeutic protocols.

It is important to distinguish between supportive therapies and definitive cures. A cure implies total eradication of the disease from the body, while prevention means reliably stopping infection from occurring. At present, only vaccines have shown strong, consistent evidence for the prevention of COVID-19, and therapeutic drugs are used in established cases to manage symptoms and reduce complications. NRICM101 may offer adjunctive benefits for symptom relief, but it is not a replacement for proven medical treatments.

The claim that drinking NRICM101 every day can cure COVID-19 or prevent infection is not supported by robust scientific evidence. While traditional remedies may play a role in holistic health approaches, relying on them exclusively for disease prevention or treatment can be risky. Individuals are encouraged to follow guidance from reputable health authorities and consult medical professionals for COVID-19 management and prevention. Misleading claims about unproven remedies can contribute to confusion and potentially endanger public health if they discourage people from seeking effective, evidence-based care.

article_content:
A recent social media post has raised concerns by linking the consumption of ice water and ice to increased vulnerability to Covid-19. The post cites the example of three Thai immigrant workers who reportedly tested positive for Covid-19 and “liked drinking ice water very much.” It further claims that drinking ice water and eating ice can harm the bronchial tubes and make individuals more susceptible to the virus.

This article examines the accuracy of these claims and explores the scientific understanding of the relationship between cold beverages and respiratory health, particularly in the context of Covid-19.

**Background and Context**

Throughout the Covid-19 pandemic, many myths and misconceptions have circulated regarding ways to prevent or contract the virus. Early in the pandemic, some social media posts claimed that drinking hot water or avoiding cold drinks could either kill the virus or prevent infection. Medical experts and public health authorities have repeatedly addressed these claims, seeking to provide clear, evidence-based guidance.

The post in question appears to revive similar concerns, specifically suggesting that consuming ice water can harm the bronchial tubes—the air passages in the lungs—and increase vulnerability to Covid-19.

**Evaluating the Evidence**

To assess the validity of the claim, it is important to consider several factors:

- **Transmission of Covid-19:** Covid-19 is caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, which primarily spreads through respiratory droplets when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or talks. The main risk factors for infection are close contact with infected individuals, poorly ventilated spaces, and lack of protective measures such as masks.

- **Effect of Ice Water on the Bronchial Tubes:** There is no scientific evidence that drinking cold beverages, including ice water, damages the bronchial tubes. The human respiratory system is well-adapted to handle a range of temperatures. When cold water is consumed, it travels down the esophagus, which is separate from the airway. Occasionally, very cold beverages may cause temporary throat discomfort in sensitive individuals, but they do not injure the bronchial tubes or lungs.

- **Susceptibility to Covid-19:** No credible scientific studies have demonstrated a link between drinking ice water or eating ice and increased susceptibility to Covid-19. The likelihood of contracting the virus is not influenced by beverage temperature but by exposure to the virus and individual risk factors such as age, underlying health conditions, and vaccination status.

- **Anecdotal Evidence:** The reference to three individuals who both enjoyed ice water and tested positive for Covid-19 does not establish causation. Many factors could explain their infections, and coincidental associations do not provide proof of a causal relationship.

**Conclusion**

The core claim that drinking ice water or eating ice harms the bronchial tubes and makes individuals more vulnerable to Covid-19 is not supported by scientific evidence. Covid-19 risk is determined by viral exposure and individual health, not by beverage temperature. Public health authorities continue to stress proven preventive measures such as vaccination, mask-wearing, hand hygiene, and physical distancing. While it is important to remain vigilant about Covid-19, avoiding ice water is not a necessary or effective measure for preventing infection.

Недавний пост в социальных сетях вызвал обеспокоенность, связав потребление ледяной воды и льда с повышенной уязвимостью к коронавирусу. В посте приводится пример трех тайских мигрантов, которые, по сообщениям, тестировались на положительный результат коронавируса и «очень любили пить ледяную воду». Далее утверждается, что употребление ледяной воды и льда может навредить бронхам и сделать людей более уязвимыми к вирусу.

Эта статья рассматривает достоверность этих утверждений и исследует научное понимание связи между холодными напитками и дыхательной системой, особенно в контексте коронавируса.

**Фон и контекст**

В ходе пандемии коронавируса циркулировали множество мифов и недоразумений, связанных с способами предотвращения или заражения вирусом. В начале пандемии некоторые посты в социальных сетях утверждали, что пить горячую воду или избегать холодных напитков может либо убить вирус, либо предотвратить заражение. Медицинские эксперты и государственные органы здравоохранения неоднократно отвечали на эти утверждения, стремясь предоставить четкую, основанную на доказательствах информацию.

В данном случае пост, похоже, воспроизводит схожие опасения, предполагая, что употребление ледяной воды может навредить бронхам — воздушным путям легких — и увеличить уязвимость к коронавирусу.

**Оценка доказательств**

Чтобы оценить достоверность утверждения, необходимо учитывать несколько факторов:

- **Передача коронавируса:** Коронавирус вызывается вирусом SARS-CoV-2, который в основном распространяется через капли, выделяемые зараженным человеком при кашле, чихании или разговоре. Основные факторы риска заражения — близкий контакт с зараженными людьми, плохо вентилируемые помещения и отсутствие защитных мер, таких как маски.

- **Влияние ледяной воды на бронхи:** Нет научных доказательств, подтверждающих, что употребление холодных напитков, включая ледяную воду, повреждает бронхи. Дыхательная система человека хорошо приспособлена к разным температурам. Когда холодная вода потребляется, она проходит по пищеводу, который отделен от дыхательных путей. Иногда очень холодные напитки могут вызывать временное дискомфорт в горле у чувствительных людей, но не наносят вред бронхам или легким.

- **Уязвимость к коронавирусу:** Нет достоверных научных исследований, подтверждающих связь между употреблением ледяной воды или льда и повышенной уязвимостью к коронавирусу. Вероятность заражения не зависит от температуры напитков, а определяется воздействием вируса и индивидуальными факторами риска, такими как возраст, наличие хронических заболеваний и статус вакцинации.

- **Анекдотические данные:** Ссылка на трех людей, которые, по сообщениям, любили пить ледяную воду и получили положительный результат на коронавирус, не доказывает причинно-следственную связь. Множество факторов может объяснить их заражение, и случайные ассоциации не подтверждают причинно-следственную связь.

**Заключение**

Основное утверждение, что употребление ледяной воды или льда вредит бронхам и делает людей более уязвимыми к коронавирусу, не подтверждается научными данными. Риск заражения коронавирусом определяется воздействием вируса и индивидуальным здоровьем, а не температурой напитков. Государственные органы здравоохранения продолжают подчеркивать проверенные меры профилактики, такие как вакцинация, ношение масок, гигиена рук и социальное дистанцирование. Хотя важно оставаться внимательным к коронавирусу, избегание ледяной воды не является необходимой или эффективной мерой для предотвращения заражения.

A social media post circulating recently claims that, starting tomorrow, people will be required to use registered EasyCards to ride the MRT. This statement has prompted confusion and concern among regular commuters, many of whom use unregistered EasyCards for daily travel. To clarify the situation, let’s examine the claim, its context, and the current policies regarding EasyCard usage and MRT access.

The EasyCard is a widely used contactless smartcard in Taiwan, primarily for public transportation, including the Taipei and Kaohsiung MRT systems, buses, and even some retail stores. EasyCards can be purchased and used anonymously, but there is also an option to register the card, which can provide benefits such as balance protection in case of loss and eligibility for certain discounts or promotions.

The core of the social media claim is that, beginning tomorrow, only registered EasyCards will be valid for MRT travel. If true, this would mark a significant change in transit policy, impacting millions of daily commuters who rely on the convenience and anonymity of unregistered cards. Such a shift would likely require extensive public notification and a robust transition period to allow all riders to register their cards.

Upon review of official MRT and EasyCard communications, there is no current announcement or evidence indicating that the use of registered EasyCards will become mandatory for MRT travel as of tomorrow. Major policy changes to public transit fare systems are typically accompanied by official press releases, signage at stations, and broad outreach through multiple channels. No such coordinated information campaign is present at this time.

In addition, the infrastructure for enforcing the use of registered EasyCards exclusively is not widely in place. MRT fare gates do not distinguish between registered and unregistered cards for entry. Registration of an EasyCard generally involves linking the card to personal information, which some users may be reluctant to do due to privacy concerns. It is unlikely that such a sweeping change would be implemented overnight without significant preparation and public discourse.

There have been discussions in recent years about enhancing security and tracking for public transportation, particularly in response to concerns about the spread of diseases or for contact tracing during emergencies. During the COVID-19 pandemic, authorities encouraged the use of registered cards for better tracking, but did not make it mandatory for MRT usage. These measures have since been relaxed, and no permanent policy has been implemented to require registration for regular transit use.

In conclusion, the social media claim that, starting tomorrow, people will be required to use registered EasyCards to ride the MRT is not supported by current official information or operational practices. MRT riders can continue to use both registered and unregistered EasyCards as usual. Commuters are advised to verify information through official sources and not rely solely on unverified social media posts. If any changes are announced in the future, they will likely be communicated clearly and with ample notice to the public.

An audio message circulating widely on social media claims to feature Dr. Chiou Shu-ti, the former head of Taiwan’s Health Promotion Administration, offering advice on how to test for and prevent COVID-19 infection. The recording suggests individuals can check their lung function by holding their breath for ten seconds and recommends keeping the throat moist as a protective measure against the virus. The message has garnered significant attention, raising concerns among public health officials and prompting questions about its authenticity and the accuracy of its claims.

**Background and Context**

Dr. Chiou Shu-ti served as the director-general of the Health Promotion Administration, a key agency under Taiwan’s Ministry of Health and Welfare, and is known for her expertise in public health policy. Since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, misinformation has proliferated on digital platforms, often featuring purported statements from reputable health figures to lend credibility. Voice messages, in particular, have become a vehicle for spreading unverified health advice, contributing to confusion and sometimes undermining official guidance.

**Analysis of the Claims**

- **Testing Lung Function by Holding Breath**

The audio message advises listeners to inhale deeply and hold their breath for at least ten seconds without discomfort or coughing to determine whether their lungs are free of infection, implying that inability to perform this task could signal COVID-19 or lung fibrosis. Medical experts universally caution that this is not a reliable method for diagnosing COVID-19 or assessing lung health. COVID-19 symptoms and complications can vary widely, and many individuals with the virus may be able to hold their breath easily, especially in early or asymptomatic stages. Conversely, people with other respiratory conditions unrelated to COVID-19 may struggle with breath-holding. Official diagnostic protocols for COVID-19 rely on laboratory testing, such as PCR or rapid antigen tests, rather than subjective self-assessment techniques.

- **Keeping the Throat Moist as a Preventive Measure**

The message also recommends frequent sips of water to keep the throat moist, suggesting this can wash the virus into the stomach where it will be destroyed by gastric acid, thereby preventing infection. This claim is not supported by scientific evidence. The main transmission route of COVID-19 is via respiratory droplets and aerosols, which can enter the body through the nose, mouth, or eyes. While staying hydrated is generally beneficial for health, it does not prevent the virus from infecting the respiratory tract. Health authorities advise proven preventive measures, such as vaccination, wearing masks, practicing hand hygiene, and maintaining physical distance.

**Authenticity of the Audio Message**

Dr. Chiou Shu-ti has publicly addressed the viral message, clarifying that she is not the source of the recording and disavowing the advice contained in it. She has urged the public to seek information from official health sources and to refrain from sharing unverified messages.

**Conclusion**

The viral audio message attributed to Dr. Chiou Shu-ti contains inaccurate and misleading health advice regarding COVID-19 prevention and detection. Neither holding one’s breath nor keeping the throat moist are effective strategies for diagnosing or preventing COVID-19 infection. The message is not authentic and does not reflect the guidance of health authorities. Members of the public are encouraged to follow official recommendations and to be cautious of misinformation, especially when it purports to come from trusted figures.

این پیام صوتی به شنوندگان توصیه می کند که با گرفتن نفس عمیق و نگه داشتن نفس خود به مدت حداقل ده ثانیه بدون ناراحتی یا کاشت، بتوانند تشخیص دهند که ریه ها آسیب دیده اند یا خیر و این ادعا را که امکان انجام این کار نبودن می تواند نشان دهنده وجود ویروس کووید-19 یا فیبروز ریه باشد. اینکه این روش به عنوان یک روش قابل اعتماد برای تشخیص ویروس کووید-19 یا ارزیابی سلامت ریه است، توسط افراد پزشکی به طور کلی به عنوان یک ادعا نادرست مورد انتقاد قرار می گیرد. علائم و عوارض ویروس کووید-19 متفاوت است و بسیاری از افراد مبتلا به این ویروس می توانند به راحتی نفس خود را نگه دارند، به خصوص در مراحل اولیه یا بدون علائم. به عکس، افرادی که دچار بیماری های تنفسی غیر مرتبط با ویروس کووید-19 هستند ممکن است دچار مشکلاتی در نگه داشتن نفس شوند. روش های رسمی تشخیص کووید-19 از جمله آزمایشات آزمایشگاهی مانند آزمایش PCR یا آزمایشات آنتی ژن سریع است، نه ارزیابی های سубجئتیو و خود ارزیابی.

- **نگه داشتن گلو مرطوب به عنوان اقدام پیشگیری**

این پیام همچنین توصیه می کند که به منظور نگه داشتن گلو مرطوب، به طور مکرر از آب بخورید و این را به عنوان یک روش پیشگیری از ابتلا به ویروس، این را توصیه می کند که ویروس را به معدة انسان بکشاند که در آن توسط اسید معده شکسته شود. این ادعا توسط اسناد علمی پشتیبانی نمی شود. روش اصلی انتقال ویروس کووید-19 از طریق قطرات تنفسی و اسپری ها است که می توانند از طریق نose، دهان یا چشم وارد بدن شوند. در حالی که نگه داشتن سیالیت به طور کلی برای سلامت مفید است، اما این امر از ورود ویروس به مسیر تنفسی جلوگیری نمی کند. مقامات بهداشتی توصیه های پیشگیری اثبات شده را مانند واکسن، پوشیدن ماسک، اقدام به بهداشت دست و حفظ فاصله فیزیکی می کنند.

**واقعی بودن پیام صوتی**

دکتر چیو شو تی به طور عمومی در مورد پیام ویروسی این پیام صوتی اظهار نظر کرده است و این را از منبع خود نمی داند و از توصیه های موجود در آن منکر است. او به عموم مردم توصیه می کند که اطلاعات را از منابع رسمی بهداشت جستجو کنند و پیام هایی که از منابع اطمینان بخش گرفته شده است را به اشتراک نگذارند.

**نتیجه گیری**

این پیام ویروسی که به نام دکتر چیو شو تی نسبت داده شده است، ادعاهای نادرست و اشتباهی درباره پیشگیری و تشخیص ابتلا به ویروس کووید-19 دارد. هیچ یک از این روش ها، نگه داشتن نفس یا نگه داشتن گلو مرطوب، به عنوان روش های مؤثر برای تشخیص یا پیشگیری از ابتلا به ویروس کووید-19 نیستند. این پیام واقعی نیست و با راهنمایی های مقامات بهداشتی همخوانی ندارد. عموم مردم به توصیه های رسمی پیروی کنند و به ویژه در مورد اطلاعاتی که به عنوان از افراد معتبر گرفته شده است، با احتیاط عمل کنند.

article_content:
A recent social media post has been circulating, claiming that a recipe for an “anti-COVID tea” has been developed by Dr. Tsung-Jung Ho. The post suggests that this tea can prevent or treat COVID-19, drawing the attention of individuals seeking alternative or natural remedies during the ongoing pandemic. This article examines the core claim, provides context, and analyzes the available evidence regarding the efficacy and legitimacy of such a recipe.

The post attributes the creation of an “anti-COVID tea” to Dr. Tsung-Jung Ho, who is presented as a medical or scientific authority. While individuals named Dr. Tsung-Jung Ho may exist in the medical or academic community, there is no widely recognized figure by this name directly associated with internationally acknowledged COVID-19 research or treatment protocols. Furthermore, official health organizations, such as the World Health Organization and national Centers for Disease Control, have not endorsed any herbal or tea-based remedies as effective preventative or therapeutic agents against COVID-19.

The notion of using herbal teas or traditional remedies to boost immunity or fight infections is not new. Throughout the pandemic, various herbal concoctions, teas, and supplements have been promoted online, often accompanied by anecdotal testimonials. Common ingredients in such teas include ginger, garlic, lemon, honey, and various herbs. While some of these ingredients may have minor health benefits—such as providing antioxidants, vitamins, or soothing sore throats—there is no scientific evidence demonstrating that any combination of herbs or teas can prevent infection with the coronavirus or cure COVID-19.

Medical consensus is clear: the most effective ways to prevent COVID-19 are vaccination, wearing masks in crowded spaces, practicing good hand hygiene, and adhering to public health guidelines. Treatments for COVID-19, especially for moderate to severe cases, involve antiviral medications, monoclonal antibodies, and supportive hospital care when necessary. No herbal tea, regardless of its ingredients or the credentials of its creator, has been proven in clinical trials to prevent or cure COVID-19.

It is important for the public to remain cautious when encountering health claims on social media, especially those lacking scientific backing or official endorsement. While drinking herbal teas is generally safe for most people and may offer comfort during illness, relying on such remedies in place of proven medical interventions can be dangerous. Additionally, individuals with certain medical conditions, allergies, or those taking specific medications should consult healthcare professionals before consuming unfamiliar herbal preparations.

In summary, the claim that Dr. Tsung-Jung Ho’s recipe of “anti-COVID tea” can prevent or treat COVID-19 is not supported by scientific evidence or official health guidance. While herbal teas may be soothing, they should not be considered a substitute for established COVID-19 prevention and treatment measures. Always seek information from reputable sources and consult healthcare professionals regarding COVID-19 management.

A video circulating on social media claims that Indian people cure COVID-19 with sacred cows. This assertion, while sensational, warrants careful examination given its implications for public health, cultural understanding, and misinformation.

To begin, India is a country where cows hold deep religious and cultural significance, especially in Hinduism. Cows are considered sacred animals by many Hindus, and their products, such as milk, ghee, and dung, play traditional roles in rituals and ceremonies. However, the intersection of religious belief and medical treatment is a complex area, particularly when modern diseases like COVID-19 are involved.

Since the emergence of COVID-19 in early 2020, India, like many nations, has grappled with the spread of misinformation regarding cures and treatments. Some fringe groups and individuals promoted various traditional remedies, including those involving cow products, as preventive or curative solutions for the coronavirus. Notably, there were isolated reports of people organizing cow dung and urine parties, believing that such practices could ward off or cure COVID-19. These events were widely covered by media and attracted criticism from medical experts who emphasized that there is no scientific basis for such claims.

Importantly, the mainstream medical community in India, including the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and the Indian Council of Medical Research, has consistently advocated for evidence-based interventions such as vaccination, mask-wearing, and social distancing. There is no official endorsement from these bodies supporting the use of cows or cow-derived products as a cure for COVID-19. While some politicians and religious leaders made statements suggesting cow products could boost immunity, these views were not adopted into government health policy.

It is crucial to distinguish between cultural practices and scientifically validated treatments. While cows are revered and their by-products are used in religious rituals, there is no credible scientific evidence that they cure COVID-19. The World Health Organization and leading health experts worldwide have repeatedly stated that there is no cure for COVID-19 apart from supportive care and approved antiviral medications, with vaccines being the most effective preventive measure.

The video in question appears to conflate cultural reverence for cows with medical efficacy, which risks spreading harmful misinformation. Such claims could deter individuals from seeking proper medical care and following public health guidelines, especially during a pandemic. The spread of these misconceptions may also perpetuate stereotypes and misunderstandings about Indian culture and practices.

In summary, while some isolated groups in India have promoted cow-related rituals as protective against COVID-19, there is no scientific or official support for the claim that Indian people cure COVID-19 with sacred cows. The majority of the population follows established medical advice, and the claim presented in the video is misleading and not representative of the broader Indian approach to COVID-19 management.

post_content: A video says that Indian people cure Covid-19 with sacred cows.
translated_post: 影片說印度人用聖牛治癒新冠肺炎。

article_content:
A recent viral video circulating on social media claims that an Indian shaman possesses the ability to treat COVID-19 by allowing patients to touch a bell tied to his genital area. The video has attracted widespread attention and sparked both curiosity and concern about traditional healing practices and the spread of health misinformation during the ongoing pandemic.

To evaluate this claim, it is important first to understand the context in which such practices arise. India is home to a rich tapestry of traditional and folk healing modalities, some rooted in centuries-old cultural beliefs. Shamans, locally known as “babas” or “tantriks” in some regions, often claim to possess supernatural powers and offer unconventional remedies for a variety of ailments. These practices, while part of regional folklore, are not recognized by mainstream medical science.

The video depicts a shaman performing a ritual, where the purported treatment for COVID-19 involves the patient touching a bell attached to the shaman’s genital area. The shaman asserts that this act can cure COVID-19 and restore health. Such claims have gained traction among certain communities, particularly in areas with limited access to formal healthcare and medical information.

A critical analysis of the claim reveals several problematic aspects. COVID-19 is caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus and is a respiratory illness that requires scientifically validated treatments. The global medical consensus, based on extensive research and clinical trials, is that COVID-19 cannot be cured through touch, rituals, or spiritual objects. Approved methods to prevent and treat COVID-19 include vaccination, antiviral medications, supportive care, and adherence to public health guidelines. Any suggestion that touching a bell affixed to a person’s genitalia could cure COVID-19 has no basis in scientific fact.

Furthermore, such practices carry potential health risks. Encouraging close physical contact, particularly in ways that violate personal boundaries or hygiene standards, can facilitate the spread of infectious diseases, including COVID-19 itself. The World Health Organization and national health authorities have consistently warned against unproven treatments and have urged the public to rely on evidence-based medicine.

The proliferation of videos and posts promoting dubious cures reflects a broader issue of misinformation in the digital age. During health crises like the COVID-19 pandemic, false claims can undermine public trust in effective interventions, discourage vaccination, and lead to dangerous behaviors. Vulnerable populations may be particularly at risk, especially where superstition, lack of education, and limited healthcare converge.

In summary, the claim that an Indian shaman can treat COVID-19 by having patients touch a bell fastened to his genital area is entirely unfounded. There is no scientific evidence to support the effectiveness of this practice, and it poses potential health risks. Individuals seeking treatment for COVID-19 are strongly advised to consult qualified medical professionals and adhere to recognized public health measures. The spread of such misinformation highlights the ongoing need for vigilance, public education, and responsible reporting during global health emergencies.

A video circulating on social media claims that Japanese medical staff regularly drink water every 15 minutes to keep their throats moist, with the belief that this practice allows gastric acid to kill COVID-19 if the virus is swallowed. This claim, which has been widely shared since the early days of the pandemic, suggests that frequent hydration can prevent infection by flushing the virus from the throat into the stomach, where it is then destroyed by gastric acid.

To evaluate this claim, it is important to consider both the scientific understanding of COVID-19 infection and the practices recommended by medical authorities in Japan and worldwide. COVID-19, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, primarily infects individuals through respiratory droplets, which enter the body via the mouth, nose, or eyes. Once inside, the virus attaches to cells lining the respiratory tract, including the throat and lungs, and begins to replicate.

The notion that simply drinking water can "wash" the virus from the throat into the stomach presumes that the virus remains localized in the throat for a significant period after exposure. However, scientific studies indicate that after initial entry, the virus can rapidly invade cells and begin replication. There is currently no evidence to suggest that frequent drinking of water can prevent infection by physically flushing the virus into the stomach.

Furthermore, while gastric acid is capable of neutralizing many microorganisms, including some viruses and bacteria, SARS-CoV-2 has not been shown to be reliably inactivated by stomach acid in the context of normal exposure. The virus can infect the upper respiratory tract before it ever reaches the stomach, and transmission primarily occurs through inhalation and contact with contaminated surfaces, rather than ingestion.

As for the claim that Japanese medical staff use this method, there is no official guidance from Japanese health authorities or infection control protocols recommending frequent water intake specifically as a preventive measure against COVID-19. Standard infection control measures in Japan, as in other countries, include mask-wearing, hand hygiene, physical distancing, and vaccination. While staying hydrated is beneficial for general health, and keeping the throat moist may help with comfort, there is no evidence that it specifically protects against COVID-19.

In summary, the claim that Japanese medical staff drink water every 15 minutes to keep the throat wet so that gastric acid can kill COVID-19 is not supported by medical evidence or official guidance. The prevention of COVID-19 is best achieved by following proven strategies such as vaccination, mask-wearing, and regular hand washing. Misinformation about simple remedies like frequent water drinking can create a false sense of security and distract from effective protective measures. It is important to rely on advice from trusted health authorities and scientific research when seeking ways to prevent infection.

Une fois à l'intérieur, le virus se fixe aux cellules recouvrant le tractus respiratoire, y compris la gorge et les poumons, et commence à se multiplier.

L'idée que boire de l'eau permette de « laver » le virus de la gorge vers l'estomac suppose que le virus reste localisé dans la gorge pendant une période significative après l'exposition. Toutefois, les études scientifiques indiquent que, après l'entrée initiale, le virus peut rapidement s'implanter dans les cellules et commencer sa reproduction. Il n'existe actuellement aucune preuve suggérant que boire fréquemment de l'eau puisse prévenir l'infection en éliminant physiquement le virus vers l'estomac.

De plus, bien que l'acidité gastrique soit capable de neutraliser de nombreux micro-organismes, y compris certains virus et bactéries, le SARS-CoV-2 n'a pas été montré être inactivé de manière fiable par l'acidité gastrique dans le contexte d'une exposition normale. Le virus peut infecter le tractus respiratoire supérieur avant même d'atteindre l'estomac, et la transmission se produit principalement par inhalation et par contact avec des surfaces contaminées, plutôt que par ingestion.

En ce qui concerne l'affirmation selon laquelle le personnel médical japonais utilise cette méthode, il n'existe pas de directives officielles des autorités sanitaires japonaises ou de protocoles de contrôle des infections recommandant spécifiquement une ingestion fréquente d'eau comme mesure préventive contre le COVID-19. Les mesures standard de contrôle des infections au Japon, comme ailleurs dans le monde, incluent le port du masque, l'hygiène des mains, le maintien de la distance physique et la vaccination. Bien que l'hydratation soit bénéfique pour la santé générale et que l'hydratation de la gorge puisse aider à la confort, il n'existe aucune preuve qu'elle protège spécifiquement contre le COVID-19.

En résumé, l'affirmation selon laquelle le personnel médical japonais boit de l'eau toutes les 15 minutes afin de garder la gorge humide, de sorte que l'acidité gastrique puisse tuer le COVID-19, n'est pas appuyée par des preuves médicales ou des directives officielles. La prévention du COVID-19 est mieux assurée en suivant des stratégies éprouvées telles que la vaccination, le port du masque et le lavage régulier des mains. Les informations erronées sur des remèdes simples, comme boire fréquemment de l'eau, peuvent créer une fausse impression de sécurité et distraire des mesures protectrices efficaces. Il est important de se fier aux conseils des autorités sanitaires de confiance et des recherches scientifiques lorsqu'on cherche à prévenir l'infection.

A video circulating on social media has sparked significant attention by claiming that China recently dispatched a chartered flight to evacuate its citizens from India. The footage, which has been widely shared across various platforms, purports to show Chinese nationals boarding an airplane under the supervision of officials, accompanied by captions and commentary suggesting a major evacuation operation is underway.

The core claim of the video is that the Chinese government organized and executed a dedicated flight to retrieve its citizens from India. This assertion has led to a wave of speculation regarding the current state of China-India relations, as well as concerns about safety and diplomatic tensions between the two countries.

To evaluate the accuracy of this claim, it is essential to consider current events, official statements, and the broader context of China-India interactions. Historically, both countries have maintained regular air travel for business, tourism, and academic purposes. However, during periods of heightened tension or crisis—such as the COVID-19 pandemic—governments worldwide, including China, did organize chartered flights to bring their citizens home from foreign countries. These evacuations were typically well-publicized, with official announcements and media coverage both domestically and internationally.

As of the present, there have been no official announcements from either the Chinese or Indian governments about a new round of evacuation flights for Chinese nationals in India. Major news outlets and government agencies have not reported any recent evacuation initiative. Routine commercial flights between China and India remain limited due to ongoing pandemic-related restrictions and diplomatic considerations, but these restrictions have been gradually easing over time.

Further scrutiny of the video in question reveals ambiguities. The footage does show passengers boarding an aircraft, but there is no verifiable evidence confirming the location as India or the passengers as Chinese nationals. No signage, airport identifiers, or clear audio in the video definitively place the event in India or link it to a Chinese evacuation effort. In the past, similar videos have been repurposed or misrepresented to fit different narratives, especially during times of geopolitical tension.

There have been isolated incidents where individuals or small groups have returned to China from India via arranged transport, often due to personal emergencies or special circumstances. These cases, however, are not equivalent to large-scale, government-coordinated evacuations and do not constitute evidence supporting the claim made in the viral video.

In summary, while the video suggests a large-scale evacuation of Chinese citizens from India via a chartered flight, there is no concrete evidence to substantiate this claim. Neither government has confirmed such an operation, and there is a lack of credible reporting or official documentation supporting the narrative presented. The available information indicates that the video is likely to be misleading or taken out of context, rather than an accurate representation of current events. As always, viewers are urged to seek information from reliable sources and exercise caution when encountering sensational claims on social media.

Potongan film tersebut, yang telah dibagikan secara luas di berbagai platform, tampaknya menunjukkan warga Tiongkok yang sedang naik ke pesawat di bawah pengawasan pejabat, lengkap dengan teks dan komentar yang menunjukkan bahwa operasi evakuasi besar sedang berlangsung.

Pernyataan utama dalam video tersebut adalah bahwa pemerintah Tiongkok mengorganisasi dan melaksanakan penerbangan khusus untuk mengambil warganya dari India. Klaim ini telah menimbulkan spekulasi yang luas mengenai hubungan Tiongkok-India saat ini, serta kekhawatiran mengenai keamanan dan ketegangan diplomatik antara kedua negara.

Untuk mengevaluasi kebenaran klaim tersebut, penting untuk mempertimbangkan peristiwa terkini, pernyataan resmi, serta konteks yang lebih luas mengenai interaksi antara Tiongkok dan India. Secara historis, kedua negara telah menjaga perjalanan udara rutin untuk tujuan bisnis, wisata, dan akademik. Namun, selama masa-masa ketegangan meningkat atau krisis—seperti pandemi virus corona—pemerintah di seluruh dunia, termasuk Tiongkok, memang mengorganisasi penerbangan charter untuk membawa warganya kembali ke negara asal dari negara lain. Evakuasi tersebut biasanya diberitakan secara luas, dengan pernyataan resmi dan liputan media domestik maupun internasional.

Saat ini, tidak ada pernyataan resmi dari pemerintah Tiongkok atau India mengenai pengiriman penerbangan evakuasi baru untuk warga Tiongkok di India. Media utama dan lembaga pemerintah tidak melaporkan adanya inisiatif evakuasi terbaru. Penerbangan komersial rutin antara Tiongkok dan India tetap terbatas karena batasan yang terkait dengan pandemi dan pertimbangan diplomatik, namun batasan tersebut secara bertahap sedang dilemaskan seiring waktu.

Pemeriksaan lebih lanjut terhadap video tersebut menunjukkan ketidakjelasan. Potongan film tersebut memang menunjukkan penumpang yang sedang naik ke pesawat, tetapi tidak ada bukti yang dapat diverifikasi mengenai lokasi di India atau identitas penumpang sebagai warga Tiongkok. Tidak ada tanda penunjuk, identifikasi bandara, atau suara jelas dalam video yang secara definitif menempatkan kejadian tersebut di India atau menghubungkannya dengan upaya evakuasi Tiongkok. Di masa lalu, video serupa sering kali diretas atau disalahartikan untuk sesuai dengan narasi yang berbeda, terutama selama masa ketegangan geopolitik.

Ada beberapa insiden terisolasi di mana individu atau kelompok kecil kembali ke Tiongkok dari India melalui transportasi yang diatur, biasanya karena keadaan darurat pribadi atau situasi khusus. Namun, kasus-kasus ini tidak setara dengan evakuasi skala besar yang terkoordinasi oleh pemerintah, dan tidak dapat dianggap sebagai bukti yang mendukung klaim dalam video yang beredar.

Secara keseluruhan, meskipun video tersebut menyiratkan evakuasi skala besar warga Tiongkok dari India melalui pesawat charter, tidak ada bukti konkret yang mendukung klaim tersebut. Tidak ada pemerintah yang mengonfirmasi operasi semacam itu, dan tidak ada laporan yang dapat dipercaya atau dokumen resmi yang mendukung narasi yang disampaikan. Informasi yang tersedia menunjukkan bahwa video tersebut kemungkinan besar salah informasi atau diambil dari konteks yang salah, bukan representasi akurat dari peristiwa saat ini. Seperti biasa, pembaca diingatkan untuk mencari informasi dari sumber yang dapat dipercaya dan berhati-hati saat menemui klaim sensasional di media sosial.

In response to a recent surge in COVID-19 cases in Taiwan, a social media post claims that Wulai, a popular tourist destination in New Taipei City, will implement road closures starting May 19 and that all tourists will be prohibited from entering indigenous tribal areas within Wulai. This article examines the accuracy of these claims and provides background on the situation.

Wulai is renowned for its hot springs, scenic mountains, and indigenous Atayal culture, drawing large crowds of both domestic and international tourists. The COVID-19 pandemic has posed unique challenges for Wulai, given its status as both a tourist hotspot and the home of several indigenous communities, which are considered particularly vulnerable due to limited healthcare resources and the risk of outbreaks in small populations.

The claim that Wulai will implement a road closure from May 19 to respond to the COVID alert is rooted in actions taken by local authorities during periods of heightened pandemic risk. In mid-May 2021, following a spike in COVID-19 cases in Taiwan and the raising of the national COVID alert to Level 3, New Taipei City officials, in coordination with tribal leaders and public health authorities, announced temporary measures to restrict access to Wulai’s tribal areas. The measures aimed to protect residents of indigenous villages, many of whom are elderly or have limited access to medical facilities.

Indeed, from May 19, checkpoints were established at key entry points to tribal areas within Wulai. These checkpoints were staffed by local police and tribal volunteers. The primary purpose was to limit the entry of non-residents, particularly tourists, to prevent the potential spread of COVID-19 into indigenous communities. Residents and those with essential business, such as delivery personnel or healthcare workers, were still permitted entry, provided they could show proof of necessity or residency.

The restriction explicitly targeted tourists and non-residents. Tourist attractions, including hot springs, hiking trails, and cultural sites within indigenous villages, were closed to the public. The decision was made in consultation with local indigenous leaders, who expressed concerns about the risk posed by outside visitors during the outbreak.

It is important to note that these restrictions were temporary and subject to change based on the evolving pandemic situation and government guidelines. Local authorities provided updates through official channels regarding the duration and scope of the closures.

In summary, the core claims of the social media post are accurate: Wulai did implement road closures restricting tourist access to tribal areas starting May 19 in response to a heightened COVID alert. These measures were part of a broader effort to safeguard vulnerable indigenous populations during a critical period of the pandemic. Tourists were indeed not allowed to enter the tribes during this period, with exceptions made only for local residents and essential personnel. The situation underscores the challenges faced by tourist-dependent communities during public health emergencies and the importance of timely, targeted interventions to protect at-risk populations.

Ta članek preučuje natančnost teh trditev in ponuja ozadje dogodka.

Wulai je znana po svojih toplih kranah, krajinah in indijski kulturi Atayal, kar jo je spremenilo v zelo obiskano kraje za domače in mednarodne turiste. Pandemija bolezni COVID-19 je predstavila posebne izzive za Wulai, ker je ne samo turistično obiskano mesto, temveč tudi domačino več indijskih skupin, ki so zelo ranljive zaradi omejenih zdravstvenih virov in tveganja za izbire v majhnih populacijah.

Trditev, da bo Wulai zatvarjal ceste od 19. maja zaradi opozorila na bolezen COVID-19, je izhajala iz dejanskih ukrepov lokalnih uradov med obdobjem povečanega tveganja zaradi pandemije. V sredini maja 2021 je po povečanem številu primerov bolezni na Tajvanu in po povečanju nacionalnega opozorila na bolezen na stopnji 3 uradni za New Taipei City, v sodelovanju s vodili indijskih skupin in javno zdravstvenimi organi objavil prečrnitev ukrepov za omejevanje dostopa do indijskih skupin v Wulai. Ukrepi so bili namenjeni zaščiti prebivalstva indijskih skupin, večinoma staršev ali ljudi z omejenim dostopom do zdravstvenih storitev.

Res, od 19. maja so bile na ključnih vhodnih točkah v indijske skupine v Wulai ustanovljene kontrolne točke. Točke so bile obiskane lokalnimi policistmi in indijskimi dobrovoljci. Glavni namen je bil omejevanje vstopa ne-prebivalcev, predvsem turistov, za preprečevanje potencialnega širjenja bolezni v indijske skupine. Prebivalci in ljudje z izjemnimi poslovno potrebami, kot so dostavni delavci ali zdravstveni delavci, so bili še vedno dovoljeni za vstop, če so lahko prikazali dokaz za potrebo ali prebivalstvo.

Omejitev je bila izrecno usmerjena proti turistom in ne-prebivalcem. Turistična atrakcija, kot so tople krene, poti za hikking in kulturni objekti v indijskih skupinah, so bile zaprte za javnost. Odločitev je bila sprejeta v sodelovanju s lokalnimi indijskimi vodili, ki so izražali skrbi glede tveganja, ki ga predstavljajo zunanji obiskovalci med izbruhom.

Vажno je opozoriti, da so te omejitve bili začasni in so se lahko spremenili glede na razvoj pandemije in vodilne smernice vlade. Lokalni uradni organi so posredujali obveščanja prek službenih kanalov o trajanju in obsegu zaprtij.

Kratek zaključek: osnovne trditve socialne omrežne objave so natančne: Wulai je res implementiral zatvarjanje cest, ki so omejevala dostop turistov do indijskih skupin od 19. maja v odgovor na povečano opozorilo na bolezen COVID-19. Te ukrepe so bili del širše napora za zaščito ranljivih indijskih skupin med kritičnim obdobjem pandemije. Turisti so res bili preprečeni, da so vstopili v indijske skupine v tem obdobju, z izjemami za lokalne prebivalce in izjemne delavce. A recent social media post claims that a Chinese medicine recipe developed by Tri-Service General Hospital can “kill all types of Covid-19 virus.” This assertion has garnered significant attention online, prompting questions about its accuracy and the broader implications for public health and Covid-19 treatment options.

Tri-Service General Hospital is a well-known medical institution in Taiwan, affiliated with the military and recognized for its contributions to healthcare, including research in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM). During the Covid-19 pandemic, many hospitals and research centers worldwide explored various treatment approaches, including repurposing existing medicines and investigating traditional remedies. In particular, some practitioners of Chinese medicine have promoted herbal formulas they claim can help mitigate symptoms or provide supportive care for patients with Covid-19.

However, the claim that a Chinese medicine recipe from Tri-Service General Hospital can “kill all types of Covid-19 virus” is extraordinary and warrants careful scrutiny. To date, there is no publicly available evidence confirming that any specific TCM formulation, whether developed at Tri-Service General Hospital or elsewhere, can directly eradicate the SARS-CoV-2 virus in the human body. While some laboratory studies have investigated the antiviral properties of certain herbs used in TCM, these studies are generally preliminary and conducted in vitro, meaning they do not necessarily translate into proven clinical outcomes for patients.

Treatment protocols for Covid-19, as recommended by global health authorities such as the World Health Organization, primarily focus on supportive care, antiviral medications, and, in severe cases, immunomodulatory therapies. While complementary therapies, including TCM, may be used alongside standard medical treatment in some countries, they are typically employed to help manage symptoms rather than as direct cures for the virus itself.

Tri-Service General Hospital has reportedly conducted research on TCM formulas for Covid-19 symptom management, aiming to reduce the severity of illness and support recovery. Some published statements suggest that certain herbal combinations could provide benefits such as reducing fever, easing cough, or improving overall wellbeing. Nevertheless, these claims are centered on symptom relief, not on killing the virus outright.

The notion that a single recipe can kill “all types” of the Covid-19 virus is also problematic. The virus has mutated over time, resulting in numerous variants. The effectiveness of any treatment against all variants would require extensive clinical trials, rigorous peer-reviewed evidence, and regulatory approval. Currently, there is no such evidence supporting the claim made in the social media post.

In summary, while traditional Chinese medicine may play a role in managing symptoms or supporting recovery from Covid-19 in some contexts, the assertion that a TCM recipe from Tri-Service General Hospital can kill all types of Covid-19 virus is not supported by scientific evidence. Individuals should rely on scientifically proven treatments and consult medical professionals for guidance, rather than relying on unverified social media claims. Misinformation about Covid-19 therapies can pose serious risks, and claims of miracle cures should always be approached with caution and critical thinking.
