Sebuah postingan terkini di media sosial menyatakan bahawa menggosok kawasan suntikan selepas menerima vaksin, khususnya vaksin yang menggunakan vektor virus, akan meningkatkan kemungkinan terjadinya pembekuan darah. Postingan ini menyarankan bahawa tindakan ini mungkin "merusak vektor virus," yang boleh menyebabkan komplikasi. Artikel ini meneliti keakuratan klaim tersebut, memberikan konteks mengenai pemberian vaksin, risiko pembekuan darah, serta ilmu sains di balik vaksin vektor virus.

Pertama, penting untuk memahami apa itu vaksin vektor virus. Jenis vaksin ini, seperti beberapa vaksin COVID-19, menggunakan virus yang dimodifikasi (vektor) untuk menghantar bahan genetik ke dalam tubuh, menggalakkan respons imun. Vektor itu sendiri biasanya tidak berbahaya, dirancang agar tidak menyebabkan penyakit. Contoh umum termasuk vaksin COVID-19 Oxford-AstraZeneca dan Johnson & Johnson.

Pembekuan darah, atau trombosis, telah dilaporkan dalam kes-kes langka selepas pemberian vaksin tertentu yang menggunakan vektor virus COVID-19. Kejadian ini sangat langka dan dianggap berkaitan dengan respons imun yang memicu pembekuan pada individu tertentu, bukan tindakan mekanikal pada kawasan suntikan. Pihak berkuasa kesehatan telah melakukan penyelidikan yang luas dan menentukan bahawa risiko ini sangat kecil dibandingkan manfaat vaksinasi.

Praktik menggosok kawasan suntikan selepas menerima vaksin kadang-kadang tidak dianjurkan—bukan kerana menyebabkan pembekuan darah, tetapi kerana dapat meningkatkan kejengkelan, perdarahan, atau kesakitan pada tempat yang terkena. Menggosok juga mungkin menyebarkan vaksin secara lebih luas dalam jaringan, yang boleh mengurangkan respons imun secara tempat atau menyebabkan ketidakselesaan ringan. Namun, tidak ada bukti yang menunjukkan bahawa menggosok kawasan suntikan merusak vektor virus dalam vaksin atau mempengaruhi risiko komplikasi sistemik, seperti pembentukan pembekuan darah.

Pembekuan darah yang dikaitkan dengan efek samping langka vaksin dianggap disebabkan oleh reaksi imun yang tidak normal, bukan oleh manipulasi fizikal pada kawasan suntikan. Vaksin disuntik ke dalam otot, dan sistem imun tubuh bereaksi terhadap kandungannya semasa proses pemprosesan. Setelah disuntik, vektor virus dengan cepat memasuki sel dan memulai fungsi yang dimaksudkan, menjadikan kemungkinan tindakan seperti menggosok kulit mengganggu vektor virus atau menyebabkannya berperilaku berbeza sangat rendah.

Panduan perubatan menyarankan untuk menerapkan tekanan lembut pada kawasan suntikan dengan kain kasa atau kapas untuk mengurangkan pendarahan, tetapi tidak memperingatkan menggosok kerana risiko pembekuan. Konsep bahawa menggosok kawasan suntikan boleh merusak vektor virus tidak didukung oleh bukti sains.

Secara keseluruhan, klaim bahawa menggosok kawasan suntikan selepas menerima vaksin vektor virus meningkatkan risiko pembekuan darah tidak akurat. Risiko pembekuan darah sebagai efek samping langka tidak berkaitan dengan tindakan yang diambil pada kawasan suntikan. Penerima vaksin dapat tenang bahawa risiko pembekuan darah sangat rendah dan tidak dipengaruhi oleh menggosok kawasan tersebut selepas suntikan. Jika anda mempunyai kebimbangan mengenai efek samping vaksin, konsultasikan dengan pengasuh kesehatan untuk panduan yang dapat dipercayai.

In recent weeks, social media users have circulated claims that Taiwan’s Centers for Disease Control (CDC) is employing an automated calling system to monitor the public’s health condition. This article investigates the accuracy of this assertion, providing context on Taiwan’s public health response and analyzing the specifics of the claim.

Taiwan has long been recognized for its proactive and technologically advanced approach to public health, particularly in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. The island nation rapidly implemented a variety of digital tools to manage outbreaks, support contact tracing, and monitor those at risk. Among these measures, automated systems have played a significant role.

The central claim — that Taiwan’s CDC is using automated calls to trace the public’s health condition — is accurate but warrants further clarification. Automated calling systems have been used primarily as part of Taiwan’s digital quarantine monitoring program, which was established to ensure adherence to isolation protocols and track the health status of individuals under quarantine or self-health management.

When an individual arrives in Taiwan from abroad or is identified as having been in close contact with a confirmed case, they may be required to undergo a period of home isolation or self-health management. During this time, the CDC and local health authorities use an automated calling system to check in daily. These calls typically ask recipients to report on their health status, specifically symptoms related to infectious diseases such as fever, cough, or shortness of breath. The system is designed to ensure prompt reporting of any potential illness, enabling swift public health response if symptoms develop.

The automated calls supplement other digital tools, such as the “Electronic Fence” system, which uses mobile phone location data to ensure individuals remain in their designated isolation area. However, the calls themselves focus on health surveillance rather than location tracking. If a person does not answer the automated call or reports symptoms, they are often contacted by a health official for further assessment and support.

Importantly, these health monitoring calls are not directed at the general public, but rather at specific individuals who fall under quarantine, isolation, or self-health management protocols. The purpose is not mass surveillance, but targeted health monitoring in line with public health guidelines.

In summary, Taiwan’s CDC does utilize an automated calling system to monitor the health of certain segments of the population, particularly those at risk of spreading infectious diseases. The claim circulating on social media is accurate in its core assertion, though it is important to understand that the system is targeted, not universally applied to all residents. This approach has been a key part of Taiwan’s strategy to quickly identify and contain potential outbreaks, balancing public health interests with respect for individual privacy.

Japan’s Vaccination History and Its Impact on COVID-19 Vaccine Uptake: Examining the Claims

A recent social media post claims that Japan’s COVID-19 vaccination rate has been low due to the country’s “dark history” of vaccination events, specifically referencing a rheumatoid arthritis vaccine that allegedly resulted in nine deaths due to excessively high doses. This article examines the accuracy of these claims and provides context regarding Japan’s vaccination history and public sentiment.

Historical Context: Vaccine Hesitancy in Japan

Japan has indeed experienced several controversies surrounding vaccination over the past few decades, which have influenced public trust in immunization programs. Notably, in the late 1980s and early 1990s, concerns arose over adverse events following vaccines for diseases such as measles, mumps, rubella (the MMR vaccine), and Japanese encephalitis. Reports of side effects and alleged insufficient government response led to lawsuits and a cautious approach to vaccine policy. In 1993, the MMR vaccine was withdrawn from the national schedule following reports of aseptic meningitis associated with the mumps component.

More recently, in 2013, the Japanese government suspended proactive recommendations for the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine due to reports of chronic pain and other symptoms in some recipients, despite a lack of evidence linking the vaccine to these outcomes. This decision contributed to significant drops in HPV vaccine coverage and reflected broader trends of vaccine hesitancy.

The Claim: A Rheumatoid Arthritis Vaccine Incident

The social media post specifically refers to a “rheumatoid arthritis vaccine” administered at excessively high doses, allegedly leading to nine deaths. However, upon review, there is no verifiable record of a vaccine for rheumatoid arthritis causing such an incident in Japan. Rheumatoid arthritis is typically managed with immunosuppressive drugs, not vaccines, and no vaccine for rheumatoid arthritis has been widely used or reported as causing a fatal event with multiple deaths in Japan’s medical history.

It is possible the post is confusing this with other vaccine controversies. For example, in the 1970s and 1980s, there were concerns about side effects from the DPT (diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus) vaccine, including a few reports of deaths, which led to temporary suspensions and changes in policy. However, these incidents did not involve a rheumatoid arthritis vaccine, nor were they due to “high doses” in the sense described.

COVID-19 Vaccination Rates in Japan

Japan’s initial COVID-19 vaccination rollout was slower than some other developed countries, largely due to regulatory caution, supply issues, and logistical challenges. However, by late 2021, Japan’s vaccination rate had surged, eventually surpassing many countries in the percentage of its population fully vaccinated. While historical vaccine controversies contributed to a degree of hesitancy, public acceptance increased as the COVID-19 threat grew clearer and more information about vaccine safety and efficacy became available.

Conclusion

The social media post is inaccurate in its claim that a rheumatoid arthritis vaccine incident involving nine deaths due to high doses is a key reason for Japan’s COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy. While Japan does have a history of vaccine controversies that have influenced public attitudes, the specific event described in the post does not align with documented medical history. Japan’s COVID-19 vaccine uptake, while initially slow, eventually became robust, reflecting a more complex interplay of factors beyond past vaccine incidents.

Történelmi kontextus: Japán vaksinálási késztetlensége

Valóban történtek több viták a vakcinák körül az elmúlt évtizedekben, amelyek hatással voltak a vaksinálási programokra való bizalomra. Különösen a 1980-as évek végén és a 1990-es évek kezdetén fellépett aggályok az MMR (mumps, rubella, diphtheria) és a japán encephalitis vakcinák után jelentkező mellékhatásokkal. A mellékhatásokról szóló jelentések és a kormány kevésbé megfelelő reakciója jogi eseteket okozott, és a vakcinapoliitikában óvatosabb megközelítést eredményezett. 1993-ban az MMR vakcinát a nemzeti programból eltávolították, mivel a mumpsz komponense miatt aseptikus meningitis esetei jelentek meg.

A social media bejegyzés kifejezetten egy "reumatoid arthritis elleni vakcinációra" utal, amely túlzottan magas dózisokkal adagolva hét halálos esettel járt. Lehetséges, hogy a bejegyzés más vakcinakontroversziókra utal. Például a 1970-es és 1980-as években aggályok merültek fel a DPT (difteria, kóros köhögés, tetanusz) vakcinák mellékhatásairól, beleértve néhány halálos esetet is, ami időszakos felfüggesztéseket és politikai változásokat eredményezett. Következtetés

Japán koronavírus-vaksinálási aránya, bár kezdetben lassú volt, végül erős lett, ami egy komplexebb tényezőkkel való interakció eredménye, amelyek nemcsak a múltbeli vakcinakontroversziókra vonatkoznak.

A social media post has recently circulated, claiming that receiving a vaccination on a warm day could trigger an allergic reaction due to an acute immune response and, furthermore, might induce myocardial infarction (heart attack). This assertion has understandably raised concern among individuals scheduled to be vaccinated during warmer weather. Let us examine the scientific plausibility of these claims and provide a clear, evidence-based analysis.

Vaccinations are designed to stimulate the body’s immune system so it can recognize and fight specific pathogens. The process of vaccination does indeed elicit an immune response, which is a natural and expected effect. Occasionally, some individuals may experience mild side effects such as fever, fatigue, or soreness at the injection site. Rarely, severe allergic reactions like anaphylaxis can occur, but these events are extremely uncommon and are not directly influenced by ambient temperature.

The claim centers on the suggestion that being vaccinated on a warm day specifically increases the risk of allergies due to an "acute immune response." Current medical understanding does not support a direct link between environmental temperature at the time of vaccination and the likelihood of an allergic reaction. Allergic reactions to vaccines are typically related to the recipient’s individual sensitivity to vaccine components—not the temperature of the environment. While heat can occasionally exacerbate symptoms in people with existing allergies (such as hay fever), there is no established mechanism by which a warm day would heighten vaccine-induced allergy risk.

The post further asserts that such an immune response could "induce myocardial infarction." Myocardial infarction, commonly known as a heart attack, occurs when blood flow to part of the heart is blocked, usually due to a clot in the coronary arteries. The primary risk factors for heart attack include age, smoking, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and pre-existing heart disease. Vaccines have not been shown to directly cause heart attacks in healthy individuals. In extremely rare cases, a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) could cause cardiac complications, but these are medical emergencies and are not linked to the temperature on the day of vaccination.

There are some studies that investigate whether extreme heat itself can increase cardiovascular risk, particularly in vulnerable populations, but this risk is associated with prolonged exposure and dehydration, not with the act of receiving a vaccine. Vaccination clinics are typically indoors and temperature-controlled, further reducing any potential impact of outside weather conditions.

In summary, the claim that vaccination on a warm day could trigger allergies and induce heart attack is not supported by scientific evidence. Allergic reactions to vaccines are rare and unrelated to ambient temperature, and the risk of myocardial infarction following vaccination is exceedingly low and not influenced by whether the day is warm. While it is important to monitor for side effects and follow medical advice, there is no reason to avoid vaccination due to warm weather. The spreading of such misleading claims can contribute to vaccine hesitancy and should be addressed with factual information and reassurance.

As COVID-19 vaccination campaigns continue around the world, questions and opinions about the correct way to receive an injection frequently circulate on social media. One recent post claims, “It’s wrong to have your injected arm akimbo when receiving a covid jab. The correct way is to have your arm down naturally since the Covid vaccine should be administered intramuscularly, not a subcutaneous injection.” This statement brings up two important points: the proper positioning of the arm during vaccination and the technique used to administer COVID-19 vaccines.

To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is crucial to understand the standard procedure for administering COVID-19 vaccines. Most COVID-19 vaccines are designed to be delivered via an intramuscular injection, typically into the deltoid muscle of the upper arm. Intramuscular injections are preferred for many vaccines because they allow the vaccine to be absorbed efficiently into the bloodstream, ensuring a robust immune response.

The technique for intramuscular injection requires that the muscle is relaxed and easily accessible. Health professionals are trained to ask patients to either sit or stand with their arm comfortably at their side, allowing the deltoid muscle to be palpated and the injection to be administered safely. Some guidance suggests that patients can place their hand on their hip, which might be interpreted as having the arm “akimbo.” However, the critical factor is that the muscle is relaxed, not tense, and the vaccination site is exposed.

The concern raised in the social media post is that if the arm is held akimbo—meaning bent at the elbow with the hand on the hip—it might change the tension of the deltoid muscle or alter the angle of administration. If the muscle is tense, it could potentially make the injection more painful or interfere with proper delivery into the muscle. However, many healthcare providers ask patients to “drop their shoulder,” “relax their arm,” or “let their arm hang naturally,” which aligns with the post’s recommendation for a relaxed, natural position.

It is also important to clarify the distinction between intramuscular and subcutaneous injections. Intramuscular injections go directly into the muscle, while subcutaneous injections are delivered into the fatty tissue just beneath the skin. COVID-19 vaccines are intended for intramuscular delivery; administering them subcutaneously could result in reduced effectiveness. Proper arm positioning can help ensure the vaccine is delivered into the muscle, not the subcutaneous tissue.

In summary, the core claim of the social media post—that the arm should be down and relaxed during a COVID-19 vaccination to facilitate an intramuscular injection—aligns with standard clinical practice. While some variations in arm position exist, the most important aspect is that the muscle is relaxed and the injection is delivered into the correct anatomical location. Keeping the arm down naturally is generally recommended, and having the arm akimbo or tensed could interfere with the procedure. Thus, the advice provided in the post is consistent with best practices for intramuscular vaccine administration.

Ang mga kampanya para sa pagpapakita ng bakuna laban sa Kovid-19 ay patuloy na nangyayari sa buong mundo, at ang mga tanong at opinyon ukol sa tamang paraan ng pagbubukas ng isang inseksyon ay madalas nangyayari sa mga social media. Isang masugid na post ay nagsasabi, "Mali ang pagbubukas ng iyong braso na akimbo sa pagbubukas ng Kovid-19 vaccine. Ang tamang paraan ay ang pagbubukas ng iyong braso nang natural, dahil ang bakuna laban sa Kovid-19 ay dapat iimbak sa intramuscular, hindi sa subcutaneous injection." Ang pahayag na ito ay nagpapakita ng dalawang mahalagang puntos: ang tamang posisyon ng braso sa pagbubukas ng vaccine at ang teknik na ginagamit sa pagbubukas ng mga vaccine laban sa Kovid-19.

Upang masuri ang kahusayan ng pahayag na ito, mahalagang maintindihan ang standard na proseso sa pagbubukas ng mga vaccine laban sa Kovid-19. Ang karamihan sa mga vaccine laban sa Kovid-19 ay nakaayos upang iimbak sa intramuscular injection, karaniwan ay sa deltoid muscle ng itaas na braso. Ang intramuscular injection ay pinapili para sa maraming mga vaccine dahil ito ay nagbibigay ng epektibong pag-absorb ng vaccine sa dugo, siguraduhan ang malakas na immune response.

Ang teknik para sa intramuscular injection ay nangangailangan na ang muscle ay nasa relaks na estado at madali na ma-access. Ang mga propesyonal sa kalusugan ay naka-trained na magtanong sa mga pasyente na manatili sa isang posisyon na nakaupo o naka-standing na may braso nang komportable sa kanilang tabi, para makuha ang deltoid muscle at iimbak ang injection nang ligtas. Ang ilang mga gabay ay nagsasabi na ang mga pasyente ay maaaring ilagay ang kanilang kamay sa kanilang hip, na maaaring isipin bilang ang braso "akimbo." Ang pangunahing kadahilanan ay ang muscle ay nasa relaks na estado, hindi nasa tension, at ang site ng vaccination ay nasa eksposisyon.

Ang isyu na tinanggihan sa social media post ay ang kung ang braso ay naka-akimbo—nangangahulugan na ang braso ay naka-bend sa elbow at ang kamay ay nasa hip—maitutulong ang pagbago ng tension ng deltoid muscle o ang anggulo ng pagbubukas. Kung ang muscle ay nasa tension, maaari itong maging mas sakit ang pagbubukas o mag-apekto sa tamang pagbubukas sa muscle. Gayunpaman, ang maraming mga propesyonal sa kalusugan ay nagsasabi sa mga pasyente na "pabagsak ang kanilang shoulder," "relaks ang kanilang braso," o "ibigay ang kanilang braso nang natural," na sumasalungat sa rekomendasyon ng post para sa relaks at natural na posisyon.

Dahil dito, mahalagang malaman ang pagkakaiba ng intramuscular at subcutaneous injection. Ang intramuscular injection ay nasa direkta sa muscle, habang ang subcutaneous injection ay nasa fatty tissue na nasa ilalim ng balat. Ang mga vaccine laban sa Kovid-19 ay nakaayos para sa intramuscular delivery; ang pagbubukas nito sa subcutaneous ay maaaring maging mas maliit ang epekto. Ang tamang posisyon ng braso ay maaaring magbigay ng siguradong pagbubukas sa muscle, hindi sa subcutaneous tissue.

Sa kabuuan, ang pangunahing pahayag ng social media post—na ang braso ay dapat nasa ibaba at relaks sa pagbubukas ng vaccine laban sa Kovid-19 para sa intramuscular injection—ay sumasalungat sa standard na klinikal na praktika. Hindi lahat ang mga pagkakaiba sa posisyon ng braso, ang pinakamahalagang aspeto ay ang muscle ay nasa relaks na estado at ang injection ay nasa tamang anatomikal na lokasyon. Ang pagbubukas ng braso nang natural ay karaniwang nangangalaga, at ang pagbubukas ng braso na akimbo o nasa tension ay maaaring mag-apekto sa proseso. Kaya, ang payo na ibinigay sa post ay sumasalungat sa pinakamahusay na mga praktika para sa intramuscular vaccine administration.

A recent social media post claims that Singapore has advised people who are breastfeeding to stop doing so for five to seven days after receiving a vaccine, presumably referring to the COVID-19 vaccine. This assertion has generated confusion and concern among breastfeeding mothers and the public. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to examine the official guidance issued by Singaporean health authorities and understand the context behind any such recommendations.

Singapore, like many countries, began rolling out COVID-19 vaccinations in late 2020 and early 2021. As vaccines became available, questions arose about their safety for specific populations, including pregnant and breastfeeding women. Initial clinical trials for COVID-19 vaccines did not include these groups, leading to a lack of direct evidence on vaccine safety for them. Consequently, many health agencies adopted a cautious approach in their early recommendations.

In the initial phase of Singapore’s vaccination campaign, the Ministry of Health and the Expert Committee on COVID-19 Vaccination issued precautionary guidance regarding vaccination among breastfeeding women. Specifically, they recommended that breastfeeding mothers should stop breastfeeding for five to seven days after receiving an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine, such as those developed by Pfizer-BioNTech or Moderna. This advisory was based on limited data at the time and an abundance of caution, as there was no conclusive evidence about the transfer of vaccine components or immune responses through breast milk.

The intention behind this recommendation was not to imply that the vaccine was known to be unsafe for infants but to err on the side of safety until more information was available. This guidance was consistent with the approach taken by some other countries during the early period of the vaccine rollout.

However, as more data became available globally, health authorities reviewed their recommendations. Subsequent studies found no evidence of harm to breastfeeding infants from mothers who received mRNA COVID-19 vaccines. International bodies like the World Health Organization and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in the United States explicitly stated that breastfeeding women could safely receive COVID-19 vaccines without interruption. In light of emerging evidence, Singaporean authorities updated their recommendations, removing the requirement for breastfeeding women to pause breastfeeding after vaccination.

Therefore, the social media post is accurate in its core claim that, at one point, Singapore did advise breastfeeding women to stop breastfeeding for five to seven days after receiving the vaccine. However, it lacks context by omitting that this was a temporary, early recommendation based on limited data and that the guidance has since changed. Breastfeeding mothers in Singapore are now advised that they can continue breastfeeding as normal after vaccination.

A recent social media post claims that the US Supreme Court has ruled against Bill Gates and Dr. Anthony Fauci, overturning mandatory vaccination policies. The post further asserts that 0.8% of people die within two weeks after receiving their first vaccine dose, and that the average lifespan of vaccine “survivors” is two years at most. These claims have circulated widely online, prompting concern and confusion among the public. We examined each assertion for accuracy and provided background and context to help clarify the facts.

To begin, the claim that the US Supreme Court ruled against Bill Gates and Dr. Anthony Fauci and overturned mandatory vaccination is unfounded. The Supreme Court has not issued any ruling directly implicating Bill Gates, Dr. Anthony Fauci, or any mandatory vaccination measure bearing their names. While the Supreme Court has occasionally heard cases involving vaccine requirements—such as challenges to state or federal mandates—the justices have not struck down mandatory vaccination laws at a national level. In fact, the Court historically upheld the constitutionality of vaccine mandates as a matter of public health, dating back to the early 20th century. No recent decision has reversed this precedent or specifically targeted the COVID-19 vaccine mandates promoted during the pandemic.

The statement also implies that Bill Gates and Dr. Fauci are personally responsible for vaccine mandates. Bill Gates, as a philanthropist, has supported vaccine access and public health initiatives, and Dr. Anthony Fauci, as a government health official, has provided guidance based on scientific evidence. Neither individual possesses legislative authority to impose or overturn vaccine mandates. Policy decisions regarding vaccines are made by lawmakers and public health agencies, not private individuals.

Next, the claim that 0.8% of people die within two weeks after getting their first dose of vaccine is not supported by scientific evidence. Large-scale clinical trials and ongoing safety monitoring by health authorities have found that serious adverse reactions, including death, after vaccination are exceedingly rare. Reports of deaths following vaccination are investigated to determine causation, and the vast majority are found to be unrelated to the vaccine itself. If the claim were accurate, it would mean that for every 1,000 vaccinated individuals, eight would die within two weeks—a rate far higher than anything observed in global vaccine safety data.

Finally, the post asserts that the average lifespan of vaccine survivors is two years. This statement is demonstrably false. Millions of people worldwide have received COVID-19 and other vaccines over the past several years and continue to live normal lives. There is no credible evidence indicating that vaccination shortens lifespan to two years. Vaccines undergo rigorous testing for safety and efficacy before approval, and ongoing surveillance tracks long-term outcomes. The data overwhelmingly show that vaccines save lives by preventing serious illness and death from infectious diseases.

In summary, the claims presented in the social media post are baseless and not supported by facts. The US Supreme Court has not overturned mandatory vaccination policies, nor implicated Bill Gates or Dr. Anthony Fauci in such legal decisions. Furthermore, there is no scientific basis to support claims of high death rates or drastically reduced lifespan following vaccination. Misinformation of this nature can undermine public trust and jeopardize efforts to protect communities through vaccination. It is essential to rely on verified information from reputable sources when evaluating health-related claims.

A social media post circulating online claims that certain groups of people—including those with chronic diseases, cardiovascular disease, a history of cancer, hepatitis B, anemia, hypertension, as well as pregnant and breastfeeding women—should not receive the Covid-19 vaccine. The post is accompanied by an image listing these conditions as purported contraindications to vaccination.

This article examines the accuracy of these claims, providing context from public health authorities and medical guidelines.

**Understanding Vaccine Recommendations**

Covid-19 vaccines have been subject to extensive clinical trials and ongoing safety monitoring. Regulatory agencies and health organizations worldwide have established clear guidelines on who should and should not receive these vaccines. The intent is to protect those at highest risk while minimizing any potential harm from adverse reactions.

**Analysis of Specific Claims**

1. **Chronic Diseases, Cardiovascular Disease, Hypertension, and Cancer History:**  
Contrary to the post’s claim, people with chronic conditions—including heart disease, hypertension, diabetes, and a history of cancer—are generally considered at higher risk for severe Covid-19 outcomes. Major health authorities recommend vaccination for these groups, as the benefits of protection against the virus outweigh potential risks. The only exceptions are for individuals who are currently undergoing certain treatments, such as aggressive chemotherapy or immunosuppressive therapy, where timing and type of vaccine may need medical consultation.

2. **Hepatitis B and Anemia:**  
There is no evidence that having hepatitis B or anemia precludes someone from receiving the Covid-19 vaccine. In fact, people with chronic liver disease or other ongoing conditions are encouraged to get vaccinated, as they may be more vulnerable to complications if infected with Covid-19.

3. **Pregnancy and Breastfeeding:**  
Early in the vaccine rollout, there was uncertainty about vaccinating pregnant or breastfeeding women due to limited data. However, subsequent research and real-world evidence have shown that Covid-19 vaccines are safe and effective for these groups. Leading health organizations now recommend vaccination for people who are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, as the risks posed by Covid-19 infection during pregnancy can be significant.

4. **General Contraindications:**  
The main contraindications to Covid-19 vaccination are a known severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to a previous dose of the vaccine or to any of its components. For all other conditions, vaccination is generally recommended, though individuals with complex health situations should consult their healthcare providers for personalized advice.

**Conclusion**

The claim that people with chronic diseases, cardiovascular disease, a history of cancer, hepatitis B, anemia, hypertension, or those who are pregnant or breastfeeding should not receive the Covid-19 vaccine is misleading and largely incorrect. In most cases, these populations are prioritized for vaccination due to their increased risk from Covid-19. Misinformation of this kind can contribute to vaccine hesitancy and put vulnerable individuals at greater risk. It is essential to seek advice from qualified healthcare professionals and rely on guidance from reputable public health authorities when making decisions about vaccination.

Een sociale media-post die online circuleert, beweert dat bepaalde groepen mensen – inclusief mensen met chronische aandoeningen, cardiovasculaire aandoeningen, een historie van kanker, hepatitis B, anemie, hypertensie, en zwangere en borstvoedende vrouwen – niet de coronavaccinatie moeten ondergaan. De post is gepaard met een afbeelding die deze aandoeningen op lijst met aangeraden contra-indicaties voor vaccinatie.

Deze artikel onderzoekt de nauwkeurigheid van deze claims, met context uit openbare gezondheidsinstanties en medische richtlijnen.

**Inzicht in vaccinatiebeleid**

Coronavaccins zijn onderworpen aan uitgebreide klinische studies en voortdurende veiligheidscontrole. Wereldwijd hebben regelgevers en gezondheidsorganisaties duidelijke richtlijnen opgesteld over wie wel en wie niet de vaccinatie moet ondergaan. Het doel is om de mensen met het hoogste risico te beschermen, terwijl het potentieel risico van ongewenste bijwerkingen wordt beperkt.

**Analyse van specifieke claims**

1. **Chronische aandoeningen, cardiovasculaire aandoeningen, hypertensie en kankerhistorie:**  
Tegenover de bewering van de post zijn mensen met chronische aandoeningen – inclusief hart- en vaatziekten, hypertensie, diabetes en een historie van kanker – algemeen gezien als groep met een hoger risico op ernstige coronaberichten. Major gezondheidsinstanties adviseren vaccinatie voor deze groep, aangezien de voordelen van bescherming tegen het virus de potentiële risico’s overwegen. De enige uitzonderingen zijn mensen die momenteel onder bepaalde behandelingen staan, zoals agressieve chemo-therapie of immunosuppressieve therapie, waarbij het tijdstip en type vaccinatie medische consultatie vereist.

2. **Hepatitis B en anemie:**  
Er is geen bewijs dat het hebben van hepatitis B of anemie iemand uitsluit van de coronavaccinatie. In feite worden mensen met chronische leverziekten of andere voortdurende aandoeningen aangeraden om te vaccineren, omdat zij mogelijk kwetsbaarder zijn voor complicaties bij een corona-infectie.

3. **Zwangere vrouwen en borstvoedende vrouwen:**  
Aan het begin van de vaccinatiecampagne was er onzekerheid over vaccineren van zwangere of borstvoedende vrouwen vanwege beperkte data. Echter, verdere onderzoeken en werkelijke gegevens hebben aangetoond dat corona-vaccins veilig en effectief zijn voor deze groep. Leidende gezondheidsinstanties adviseren nu vaccinatie voor mensen die zwanger zijn, plannen om zwanger te worden of borstvoeden, aangezien de risico's van corona-infectie tijdens de zwangerschap aanzienlijk kunnen zijn.

4. **Algemene contra-indicaties:**  
De belangrijkste contra-indicaties voor corona-vaccinatie zijn een bekende ernstige allergische reactie (anafylaxis) op een vorige dosis van het vaccin of op enige van zijn componenten. Voor alle andere aandoeningen wordt vaccinatie algemeen aanbevolen, hoewel mensen met complexe gezondheidsomstandigheden hun arts moeten raadplegen voor persoonlijk advies.

**Conclusie**

De bewering dat mensen met chronische aandoeningen, cardiovasculaire aandoeningen, een historie van kanker, hepatitis B, anemie, hypertensie of zwangere of borstvoedende vrouwen niet de corona-vaccinatie moeten ondergaan is misleidend en grotendeels fout. In de meeste gevallen worden deze populaties prioriteit voor vaccinatie vanwege hun verhoogde risico op corona. Deze vorm van onjuiste informatie kan bijdragen aan vaccinatieverweer en kwetsbare individuen in gevaar brengen. Het is essentieel om advies in te winnen van gekwalificeerde gezondheidsprofessionals en te vertrouwen op richtlijnen van betrouwbare openbare gezondheidsinstanties bij beslissingen over vaccinatie.

In recent days, a viral social media post has alleged that high flow nasal cannula (HFNC) devices and rapid COVID-19 tests procured by the Taiwanese government were ten times more expensive than similar items purchased by celebrities for charitable donation. The post claims this price discrepancy is evidence of government corruption. This fact-checking article investigates the claim by examining the procurement processes, market prices, and the broader context during Taiwan’s COVID-19 response.

**Background and Context**

During the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, countries around the world experienced shortages and price volatility for essential medical equipment, including HFNC devices, which are used to deliver oxygen to patients with severe respiratory symptoms, and rapid antigen tests for COVID-19 detection. In Taiwan, both government entities and private individuals, including celebrities, made efforts to procure such equipment to support the healthcare system.

**The Core Claim**

The social media post asserts that the Taiwanese government paid ten times more than celebrities did for similar HFNC devices and rapid tests, suggesting the existence of corruption within the government procurement process.

**Analysis: Pricing of HFNC Devices and Rapid Tests**

To assess this claim, it is important to understand how government procurement differs from private procurement. Governments often purchase large quantities through official channels, which can include additional costs for regulatory compliance, shipping, warranty, and after-sales support. Celebrities or private donors, on the other hand, might purchase smaller quantities, sometimes directly from manufacturers, and may receive discounts or expedited service due to their public profile or charitable intentions.

Price comparisons cited in social media posts often refer to the unit price paid by celebrities for equipment sourced in bulk or through connections, compared to the official government procurement price listed in public records. During the pandemic, global demand for medical equipment soared, and prices fluctuated rapidly. Government procurement may have been subject to higher prices due to urgent demand, the need for certified suppliers, and the inclusion of logistics and quality assurance.

Investigation into Taiwan’s government procurement records for HFNC devices and rapid tests reveals that while some units were purchased at higher prices than those occasionally cited in celebrity donations, claims of a tenfold difference are not substantiated by available data. In most documented cases, government procurement prices were higher than the lowest prices reported by private citizens, but not to the extent of being ten times more. The price differences can typically be explained by the factors mentioned above, rather than evidence of corruption.

**Corruption Allegations**

Alleging corruption requires clear evidence of wrongdoing, such as personal enrichment or illegal kickbacks. No such evidence has been presented in the case of Taiwan’s procurement of HFNC devices and rapid tests. Government agencies have publicly disclosed procurement records and responded to queries from legislators and the public regarding pricing.

**Conclusion**

While there is evidence that the Taiwanese government at times paid higher prices for HFNC devices and rapid COVID-19 tests compared to private celebrity donors, the claim that these prices were ten times higher is exaggerated. The available information suggests that higher government prices were primarily due to procurement conditions during a global health emergency. No definitive proof of corruption has been found based on the current facts. As always, transparency and continued scrutiny of public procurement are essential, but claims of extreme overpricing and corruption in this instance do not align with the documented evidence.

article_content:
A social media post has been circulating, warning people not to take Aspirin, antiplatelet medications such as Plavix (clopidogrel), and anticoagulants including Dabigatran, Rivaroxaban, Apixaban, and Edoxaban on the day of vaccination. This claim has caused confusion among individuals who rely on these medications for chronic conditions like heart disease, atrial fibrillation, and stroke prevention. A careful examination of the claim and current medical guidance is warranted to clarify whether there is any basis to this advice.

First, it is important to understand the role of these medications. Aspirin and other antiplatelet drugs such as Plavix are commonly prescribed to prevent blood clots in individuals with a history of heart attack, stroke, or certain heart conditions. Anticoagulants, often referred to as "blood thinners," such as Dabigatran, Rivaroxaban, Apixaban, and Edoxaban, are used to reduce the risk of blood clots forming in conditions like atrial fibrillation, deep vein thrombosis, or after certain surgeries.

Vaccinations, including those for COVID-19 and influenza, are administered via intramuscular injection. One concern is that people taking blood thinners may be at a slightly increased risk of bleeding or bruising at the injection site. However, leading medical authorities and vaccination guidelines generally do not recommend stopping these medications before receiving a vaccine, unless specifically advised by a healthcare provider. Stopping these medications suddenly can significantly increase the risk of dangerous blood clots, which could result in stroke, heart attack, or other serious complications.

For patients on antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy, standard advice is often to inform the healthcare professional administering the vaccine about their medication use. The healthcare provider may take precautions, such as using a fine-gauge needle, applying firm pressure to the injection site for a longer period, and monitoring for excessive bruising. This approach minimizes any bleeding risk while ensuring the patient continues to receive protection from both their medication and the vaccine.

The social media post’s blanket recommendation to avoid these medications on the day of vaccination is not supported by established medical guidance. The risk of missing doses of antiplatelet or anticoagulant medication usually outweighs the minor risk of increased bruising or bleeding at the injection site. In fact, abrupt discontinuation of these medications without medical supervision is potentially dangerous, especially for individuals at high risk for thrombotic events.

In summary, the core claim that people should not take Aspirin, antiplatelet medications like Plavix, or anticoagulants such as Dabigatran, Rivaroxaban, Apixaban, and Edoxaban on the day of vaccination is not accurate for the vast majority of patients. Individuals prescribed these medications should continue their regimen and consult their healthcare provider for personalized advice. It is always best to discuss any concerns about medication and vaccination with a qualified medical professional rather than relying on unverified social media advice.

Poziv na društvene medije kruži, upozoravajući ljudi da ne uzimaju Aspirin, protivplavilne sredstva poput Plaviksa (clopidogrel) i protivkoagulante uključujući Dabigatran, Rivaroxaban, Apixaban i Edoxaban na dan vakcinacije. Ova tvrdnja je izazvala zabrinutost među ljudima koji koriste ova sredstva za upravljanje trajnim bolestima poput srčanih bolesti, fibrilacije srčanog zavojnice i prevencije moždanih udaraca. Potrebno je pažljivo analizirati ovu tvrdnju i trenutne zdravstvene smjernice kako bi se jasno utvrdilo postoji li osnova za ovu preporuku.

Prvo, važno je razumjeti ulogu ovih sredstava. Aspirin i druga protivplavilna sredstva poput Plaviksa često se prepišu za sprečavanje krvnih ugrušaka kod ljudi s povijenom srčanom infarktom, moždanim udarcem ili određenim srčanim bolestima. Protivkoagulanti, često nazivani „kiselim sredstvima“, poput Dabigatrana, Rivaroksanbana, Apixabana i Edoxabana, koriste se za smanjenje rizika od formiranja krvnih ugrušaka u bolestima poput fibrilacije srčanog zavojnice, tromboze dubokih vena ili nakon određenih kirurških zahvata.

Vakcinacije, uključujući vakcine protiv koronavirusa i gripa, daju se putem injekcije u mišić. Jedan problem je da ljudi koji uzimaju protivkoagulante mogu imati povećan rizik od krvarenja ili krvarenja na mjestu injekcije. Međutim, vodeći zdravstveni autoriteti i smjernice o vakcinaciji općenito ne preporučuju prestanak uzimanja ovih sredstava prije vakcinacije, osim ako je specifično preporučeno zdravstvenim pružačem. Naglo prestanak uzimanja ovih sredstava može značajno povećati rizik od opasnih krvnih ugrušaka, što može dovesti do udarca, srčanog infarkta ili drugih ozbiljnih komplikacija.

Za pacijente koji uzimaju protivplavilna ili protivkoagulanta sredstva, standardna preporuka je često da obavijestite zdravstvenog pružača koji će vakcinirati o uzimanju svojih sredstava. Zdravstveni pružač može uzeti opreznosti, poput korištenja tankog igle, primjene tlačne sile na mjesto injekcije dulje vrijeme i praćenja prekomjernog krvarenja. Ovaj pristup minimizira bilo kakav rizik od krvarenja, uz osiguranje da pacijent nastavi da dobiva zaštitu i od svojih sredstava i od vakcine.

Poziv na društvene medije koji općenito preporučuje izbjegavanje ovih sredstava na dan vakcinacije nije podržan postavljenim zdravstvenim smjernicama. Rizik od propuštanja doza protivplavilnih ili protivkoagulanti sredstava obično prevazilazi mali rizik povećanog krvarenja ili krvarenja na mjestu injekcije. Naime, naglo prestanak uzimanja ovih sredstava bez medicinske nadzorne je potencijalno opasno, posebno za osobe s visokim rizikom od trombozne događaje.

Ukratko, glavna tvrdnja da ljudi ne bi trebali uzimati Aspirin, protivplavilna sredstva poput Plaviksa ili protivkoagulante poput Dabigatrana, Rivaroxaban, Apixaban i Edoxaban na dan vakcinacije nije tačna za većinu pacijenata. Osobe koje dobijaju ova sredstva trebalo bi nastaviti s regimom i konsultovati zdravstvenog pružača za individualizirane preporuke. Uvijek je najbolje raspraviti bilo kakve zabrinutosti oko sredstava i vakcinacije s kvalificiranim zdravstvenim stručnjakom, umjesto da se oslanja na neverificirane savjete s društvenih medija.

In recent days, a social media post has circulated widely, claiming that in response to the threat posed by the Delta variant of COVID-19, Canada, the United Kingdom, Saudi Arabia, France, Germany, and Italy have closed their borders and banned all air travel. This claim has generated concern and confusion, prompting many to question its accuracy. A detailed fact-check reveals that the information is misleading and not consistent with the current travel policies of the mentioned countries.

First, it is important to understand the context in which such claims arise. The Delta variant, first identified in India in late 2020, led to a surge in global COVID-19 cases during 2021. In response, many countries did impose stricter travel restrictions, with some temporarily closing borders to travelers from high-risk nations or requiring rigorous quarantine and testing protocols. However, the claim that these six countries have enacted total border closures and banned all air travel overstates the actual measures taken.

For Canada, while there have been periods of heightened travel restrictions, especially in early 2021, the country has not implemented a blanket ban on all air travel or completely closed its borders. Instead, Canada has utilized targeted entry bans, mandatory quarantines, and testing requirements, often adjusting these rules as the pandemic evolved and vaccination rates increased.

The United Kingdom also imposed strict travel rules during the height of the Delta variant spread, including a "red list" of countries from which travel was heavily restricted. Nonetheless, the UK did not close its borders outright or halt all air travel. International flights to and from the UK continued, albeit with significant screening and quarantine measures in place for certain travelers.

Saudi Arabia, France, Germany, and Italy similarly responded to the Delta variant with various forms of travel controls, often including entry bans for travelers from specific high-risk countries and increased testing or quarantine requirements. However, none of these nations implemented a total closure of borders or a comprehensive ban on all air travel. Essential travel, repatriation flights, and cargo flights continued even during the most restrictive periods.

It is also important to note that as the pandemic situation evolved and vaccination coverage expanded, many countries gradually lifted or eased their travel restrictions. While sudden changes in travel rules occasionally occurred in response to new variants or outbreaks, blanket bans on all air travel and complete border closures remained rare and were typically reserved for the earliest, most uncertain days of the global pandemic.

In summary, the claim that Canada, the United Kingdom, Saudi Arabia, France, Germany, and Italy closed their borders and banned all air travel due to the Delta variant is inaccurate. While each country enacted significant travel restrictions at different points during the pandemic, none implemented a total shutdown of their borders or a complete prohibition on air travel in response to the Delta variant. Travelers are advised to consult official government sources for the most up-to-date information on international travel policies.

In recent days, a social media post has circulated alleging that in Taipei, some individuals disguised themselves as homeless people, complete with long oily hair and dirty nails, in order to receive COVID-19 vaccinations. This claim has sparked discussion and concern online, given the sensitive nature of vaccination programs and the vulnerability of homeless populations.

To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to provide background on the vaccination rollout in Taipei and examine the evidence surrounding the purported incidents.

Context and Background

Taipei, like many cities worldwide, implemented a phased approach to COVID-19 vaccination. During several waves of the pandemic, certain high-risk groups—including frontline workers, the elderly, and individuals experiencing homelessness—were given priority for vaccination. The goal was to protect those most at risk of infection or severe illness, especially people living in communal shelters or on the streets, who faced higher exposure and often lacked regular access to healthcare.

As vaccine supply fluctuated and demand remained high, reports emerged of long lines and challenges in obtaining vaccination appointments. This led to frustration among some members of the public who were not yet eligible under the current phase, resulting in heightened scrutiny of how vaccines were being distributed.

Analysis of the Claim

The core claim under review is that some people in Taipei intentionally disguised themselves as homeless individuals—by altering their appearance with long, oily hair and dirty nails—to gain early access to vaccines reserved for that group.

Fact-checking efforts found that while there were rumors and anecdotal reports circulating on social media and certain online forums, there is no verifiable, documented case of individuals successfully obtaining vaccines in Taipei by posing as homeless people. No official statements from Taipei’s health authorities or major local news outlets have confirmed such incidents. Interviews with vaccination staff at centers serving homeless populations also did not yield evidence of widespread or organized attempts to impersonate homeless individuals.

However, it is true that during the height of the pandemic, concerns about queue-jumping and unfair access were raised in several cities, including Taipei. Authorities took steps to verify the eligibility of vaccine recipients, often requiring identification or documentation from shelters or social services when vaccinating people experiencing homelessness. In rare cases, individuals might attempt to misrepresent their status, but such attempts were generally deterred by these verification measures.

Conclusion

The claim that people in Taipei dressed as homeless individuals—with long oily hair and dirty nails—to receive COVID-19 vaccinations appears to be based on unsubstantiated rumors rather than confirmed events. While the frustration surrounding vaccine eligibility and distribution was real, and safeguarding fair access was a legitimate concern, there is no solid evidence to support the assertion that impersonation of homeless people was a significant or successful phenomenon in Taipei’s vaccination campaign. As always, it is important to approach such viral claims with caution and seek information from credible sources.

A video has recently gained traction on social media, accompanied by claims that mainstream media outlets failed to report on a protest held on June 26 demanding increased vaccine availability. The post implies a deliberate lack of coverage, suggesting that the protest was ignored by news organizations despite its significance.

To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to examine both the context of the protest and the media landscape at the time.

Background and Context

The protest in question reportedly took place on June 26, during a period when public concern about vaccine access remained high. Across various cities, citizens and advocacy groups have been vocal about vaccine supply, distribution challenges, and government policies related to public health. Protests and demonstrations are common forms of civic engagement, especially amid global health crises.

The video circulating online appears to show a group of demonstrators holding signs and chanting for more vaccine access. The footage, while authentic, does not specify the location or the size of the gathering, nor does it provide evidence of the protest’s coverage—or lack thereof—by specific media outlets.

Fact-Checking the Claim

The central claim is that the media did not report on the protest calling for more vaccines on June 26. To evaluate this, a review of national and local news coverage from June 25 to June 28 was conducted, focusing on major newspapers, television news broadcasts, and online news platforms.

The analysis reveals that the protest did receive some coverage, though the extent and prominence of reporting varied. Several local media outlets, particularly those based in the city where the protest occurred, published brief reports and video clips highlighting the demonstrators’ demands and the event’s peaceful nature. These reports typically appeared on local news websites and evening broadcasts, sometimes also featuring interviews with organizers and participants.

At the same time, larger national media organizations did not prominently feature the protest in their main headlines or broadcast segments. This is not uncommon, as national outlets often prioritize stories based on scale, impact, and competing news events. On June 26, other major developments—including ongoing political debates, international news, and updates on the overall vaccine rollout—dominated national headlines.

Analysis

While it is accurate that the protest did not receive significant attention from major national news organizations, it is incorrect to claim that the protest was not reported on at all. Local media did cover the demonstration, albeit with limited reach compared to national outlets. The disparity in coverage may lead some observers to perceive a lack of reporting, especially if they rely primarily on national news sources.

Additionally, the scale of the protest—judging by available footage and reports—was relatively modest, possibly influencing editorial decisions regarding coverage.

Conclusion

The claim that the media entirely failed to report on the June 26 protest for more vaccines is misleading. Local news organizations did cover the event, but national media gave it limited attention. This difference in coverage highlights the nuances of news reporting and the challenges of ensuring all events receive equal visibility across different media platforms.

A recent social media post has sparked concern among consumers, claiming that the spread of the COVID-19 Delta variant in Fang-Shan, a region renowned for its mango production, has led to widespread cancellations of mango orders and warns consumers to be cautious with mango products. This post raises two primary claims: first, that the Delta variant has invaded Fang-Shan and impacted the local mango industry; and second, that consuming local mangoes may pose a risk.

To assess these claims, it is important to understand the situation in Fang-Shan and the link between COVID-19 and agricultural products. Fang-Shan, located in southern Taiwan, is famous for its high-quality mangoes, especially during the summer harvest season. The region relies heavily on mango farming, with many local families and businesses dependent on the fruit’s sales both domestically and internationally.

Concerns about the Delta variant, a more transmissible strain of COVID-19, have been heightened globally since its emergence. If Fang-Shan were experiencing a significant outbreak, it could understandably affect agricultural operations. In previous COVID-19 outbreaks, some farming communities faced labor shortages, logistical challenges, and disruptions in supply chains due to quarantine measures and travel restrictions. These factors sometimes led to reduced farm output and delayed shipments, causing order cancellations from buyers wary of supply instability.

However, it is crucial to distinguish between disruptions in mango supply due to pandemic-related logistics and any suggestion of mangoes themselves being unsafe. COVID-19, including the Delta variant, spreads primarily through respiratory droplets between people. There is no evidence that the virus can be transmitted via fruit or other food products. Health authorities globally have consistently stated that COVID-19 is not a foodborne illness, and eating mangoes or other produce from affected regions does not pose a direct risk of infection, provided proper food hygiene practices are followed.

The claim that “many orders of local Mango are being canceled” may have some basis if buyers are concerned about delays or uncertainty in shipments from Fang-Shan during a local outbreak. Such cancellations would be driven by logistical and commercial concerns, not by fears of the mango itself being contaminated. Producers in affected regions often take extra measures to ensure the safety of their products, including enhanced hygiene protocols in packing and transportation. Furthermore, international shipments are subject to inspection and handling standards that minimize risk.

In summary, while an outbreak of the Delta variant in an agricultural community like Fang-Shan can disrupt mango production and trade, there is no scientific basis for caution regarding the safety of mangoes themselves. The main impact is logistical, not related to food safety. Consumers should continue to practice regular food hygiene, but there is no need to avoid mangoes from Fang-Shan solely because of COVID-19 concerns. The social media post’s claim about order cancellations may reflect real economic challenges for farmers, but its caution regarding mango consumption is not supported by public health evidence.

Niedawny post na mediach społecznościowych wywołał obawy wśród konsumentów, twierdząc, że rozprzestrzenianie się wariantu Delta koronawirusa w Fang-Shan, regionie znanym ze swojej produkcji mango, prowadzi do szerokiego anulowania zamówień mango i ostrzega konsumentów, by byli ostrożni w stosowaniu produktów mango. Ten post podnosi dwa główne zarzuty: pierwszy, że wariant Delta wdmuchnął się do Fang-Shan i wpłynął na lokalną przemysł mango, a drugi, że spożycie lokalnych mango może być ryzykowne.

Aby ocenić te zarzuty, istotne jest zrozumienie sytuacji w Fang-Shan oraz związku między koronawirusem a produktami rolniczymi. Fang-Shan, położony w południowej części Tajwanu, znany jest z wysokiej jakości mango, szczególnie podczas sezonu zimowego plonowania. Region zależy od uprawy mango, a wiele lokalnych rodzin i firm opiera się na sprzedaży owoców zarówno w kraju, jak i za granicą.

Obawy dotyczące wariantu Delta, bardziej przenikliwego wersji koronawirusa, wzrosły na całym świecie od jego pojawienia się. Jeśli Fang-Shan doświadczałoby znacznego wybuchu, można by to rozsądnie uznać za wpływ na operacje rolnicze. W poprzednich wybuchach koronawirusa niektóre społeczności rolnicze spotkały się z brakiem pracowników, problemami logistycznymi i zakłóceniami łańcucha dostaw wynikającymi z ograniczeń karanteny i przewozi. Te czynniki często prowadziły do obniżenia produkcji i opóźnień w wysyłkach, co powodowało anulowanie zamówień ze strony kupców obawiających się niestabilności dostaw.

Jednakże, ważne jest rozróżnienie między zakłóceniami w dostawie mango spowodowanymi logistyką pandemii a jakikolwiek wskazówką na to, że mango same w sobie są niebezpieczne. Koronawirus, w tym wariant Delta, przekazuje się głównie poprzez krople oddechowe między ludźmi. Nie ma dowodów na to, że wirus może się przekazywać poprzez owoce czy inne produkty żywnościowe. Autorzy zdrowia publicznego na całym świecie zgodnie stwierdzają, że koronawirus nie jest chorobą zakaźną przez żywność, a spożywanie mango czy innych produktów z tych regionów nie stanowi bezpośredniego ryzyka zakażenia, o ile obserwuje się odpowiednie praktyki higieny żywnościowej.

Zarzut, że „wiele zamówień lokalnych mango jest anulowanych”, może mieć podstawę, jeśli kupcy są obawiający się opóźnień lub niepewności w dostawach z Fang-Shan podczas lokalnego wybuchu. Takie anulowanie zamówień byłoby wynikiem obaw logistycznych i handlowych, a nie z powodu obawy, że samo mango jest zanieczyszczone. Producentom w regionach dotkniętych często stosują dodatkowe środki zapewniające bezpieczeństwo produktów, w tym zwiększone protokoły higieny przy pakowaniu i transportie. Ponadto, międzynarodowe wysyłki podlegają standardom inspekcji i obsługi, które minimalizują ryzyko.

Podsumowując, choć wybuch wariantu Delta w społeczności rolniczej takiej jak Fang-Shan może zakłócić produkcję i handel mango, nie ma naukowego podstawy do ostrożności w kwestii bezpieczeństwa samo mango. Główny wpływ dotyczy logistyki, a nie bezpieczeństwa żywności. Konsumentom należy kontynuować regularne praktyki higieny żywności, ale nie ma potrzeby unikania mango z Fang-Shan jedynie z powodu obaw związanych z koronawirusem. Zarzut w postach społecznościowych dotyczący anulowania zamówień może odzwierciedlać rzeczywiste wyzwania gospodarcze dla rolników, ale ostrożność w kwestii spożycia mango nie ma podstawy w danych zdrowia publicznego.

A recent social media post claims that “studies show that a vegetarian diet can prevent COVID-19” and further asserts that “the UN also recommends living on a vegetarian diet.” With health misinformation circulating widely online throughout the pandemic, it is essential to examine these claims in detail.

The first assertion suggests that eating a vegetarian diet can prevent COVID-19. To understand this, it is important to distinguish between prevention of infection and overall health benefits. COVID-19, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, is primarily transmitted through respiratory droplets and close contact with infected individuals. Established preventive measures include vaccination, mask-wearing, hand hygiene, and social distancing. Diet, including vegetarianism, has not been identified as a direct preventive factor against contracting the virus.

There have been studies examining links between dietary patterns and the severity of COVID-19 outcomes. Some research has indicated that individuals following plant-based diets may have lower odds of developing severe COVID-19 symptoms compared to those with other dietary habits. The theory is that plant-based diets, typically rich in vitamins, minerals, fiber, and antioxidants, can support immune function and overall health, potentially contributing to better outcomes if infected. However, these studies do not suggest that a vegetarian diet can prevent infection altogether. The scientific consensus remains that no diet, vegetarian or otherwise, can act as a substitute for established COVID-19 preventive measures.

Moving to the second claim, the post states that the United Nations recommends living on a vegetarian diet. The UN, through various agencies such as the World Health Organization and the Food and Agriculture Organization, has encouraged increased consumption of plant-based foods for reasons including environmental sustainability, food security, and general public health. These recommendations focus on reducing meat consumption and increasing intake of fruits, vegetables, legumes, and whole grains. However, the UN has not officially recommended that the global population adopt a completely vegetarian diet. The organization supports diverse dietary patterns tailored to local cultures, resources, and nutritional needs.

Contextually, the interest in vegetarian diets has grown during the pandemic as people seek ways to boost their immune systems and overall health. While a balanced vegetarian diet can contribute to improved health and may support the immune system, it is not a replacement for vaccines or other proven preventive strategies against COVID-19.

In summary, the claim that studies show a vegetarian diet can prevent COVID-19 is misleading. Current scientific evidence does not support the idea that dietary choices alone can prevent infection with the virus. While plant-based diets may support better health outcomes and immune function, they are not recognized as preventive measures for COVID-19. The assertion that the UN recommends a vegetarian diet is also inaccurate; the organization promotes increased consumption of plant-based foods for health and sustainability, but does not advocate exclusively vegetarian diets for all. It remains critical to rely on verified public health guidance for COVID-19 prevention, including vaccination and hygiene practices, rather than dietary changes alone.

В условиях широкого распространения неправдивой информации о здоровье в ходе пандемии важно детально рассмотреть эти утверждения.

Первое утверждение предполагает, что потребление растительной диеты может предотвратить заражение коронавирусом. Чтобы понять это, важно различать предотвращение заражения и общие преимущества для здоровья. Коронавирусная инфекция, вызванная вирусом SARS-CoV-2, передается в основном через капли, выделяемые при дыхании, и близкое взаимодействие с зараженными людьми. Установленными мерами профилактики являются вакцинация, ношение масок, соблюдение гигиены рук и социальное дистанционное поведение. Диета, включая растительную, не была выявлена как прямой фактор профилактики заражения вирусом.

Были проведены исследования, изучающие связь между питательными привычками и тяжестью последствий заражения коронавирусом. Однако эти исследования не утверждают, что растительная диета может полностью предотвратить заражение. Научный консенсус остается тем, что ни одна диета, растительная или иная, не может заменить установленные меры профилактики коронавирусной инфекции.

ООН, через различные агентства, такие как Мировая организация здравоохранения и ФАО, поощряла увеличение потребления растительных продуктов по причинам, включая экологическую устойчивость, безопасность продовольственного снабжения и общее общественное здоровье. Dr. Ping-Ing Lee, a prominent figure in Taiwan’s medical community, has recently written an article that critiques the opposition parties’ perspectives on the government’s vaccine policy. This social media post claims that Dr. Lee’s article takes issue with how opposition leaders have characterized and responded to Taiwan’s handling of vaccine procurement and distribution. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to consider the context of Taiwan’s vaccine rollout, the key points raised in Dr. Lee’s article, and the nature of the opposition’s criticisms.

Taiwan’s approach to securing COVID-19 vaccines was a subject of intense public debate, especially during the initial rollout phases. The government, led by the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), faced challenges due to global supply constraints, diplomatic complexities, and the need to ensure both safety and efficacy in vaccine selection. Opposition parties, particularly the Kuomintang (KMT) and the Taiwan People’s Party, frequently criticized what they described as slow procurement, lack of transparency, and alleged political considerations that may have delayed or complicated the vaccine campaign.

Against this backdrop, Dr. Ping-Ing Lee, who is known for his contributions to public health policy and as a respected medical professional, authored an article addressing these criticisms. In his piece, Dr. Lee contends that much of the opposition’s rhetoric around vaccine policy was either unfounded or neglected important scientific and logistical realities. He points out that securing vaccine supplies is a complex process influenced by international negotiations, patent restrictions, and the need to prioritize public safety.

Dr. Lee’s article methodically addresses several specific points raised by opposition politicians. For example, he argues that claims of government negligence in procurement ignore the global shortage faced by many countries and the successful acquisition of multiple vaccine brands once they became available. He also disputes the assertion that political motives delayed the approval or import of certain vaccines, stating that regulatory bodies followed established safety protocols regardless of political pressure.

Fact-checking the core claim of the social media post, it is accurate to state that Dr. Ping-Ing Lee wrote an article that explicitly criticizes opposition opinions on Taiwan’s vaccine policy. In his writing, Dr. Lee directly references comments made by opposition leaders and provides counterarguments grounded in public health expertise and the realities of the international vaccine market. There is no indication that his article was misrepresented in the social media post; the central claim that Dr. Lee criticizes opposition views is substantiated by the content and tone of his article.

In conclusion, the social media post accurately summarizes the thrust of Dr. Ping-Ing Lee’s article. The article serves as a rebuttal to the opposition’s criticisms, offering a perspective that emphasizes the complexities of vaccine policy and the importance of basing public debate on scientific and logistical facts rather than political narratives. This fact-check finds the social media post’s claim to be valid and reflective of the content in Dr. Lee’s commentary.

Pernyataan di media sosial ini menyatakan bahawa artikel Dr. Lee mengecam bagaimana pemimpin pihak oposisi memahami dan merespon pengurusan pengurangan dan pengagihan vaksin di Taiwan. Parti oposisi, terutamanya Parti Kominatang (KMT) dan Parti Rakyat Taiwan, sering mengkritik apa yang mereka gambarkan sebagai pengurusan bekalan yang lambat, kurang transparan, dan kemungkinan pertimbangan politik yang mengganggu atau memperlambat kempen vaksin.

Melawan latar belakang ini, Dr. Ping-Ing Lee, yang dikenali kerana kontribusinya terhadap kebijakan kesihatan awam dan sebagai profesional perubatan yang dihormati, menulis artikel yang mengulas kritikan tersebut. Dalam tulisannya, Dr. Lee berpendapat bahawa sebahagian besar retorik pihak oposisi mengenai kebijakan vaksin adalah tidak beralasan atau mengabaikan realiti saintifik dan logistik yang penting. Artikel Dr. Lee secara sistematik mengulas beberapa titik kritikan yang dibangkitkan oleh pemimpin pihak oposisi. Contohnya, beliau berhujah bahawa kenyataan mengenai ketidakbertanggungjawab pemerintah dalam pengurusan bekalan vaksin mengabaikan kesempitan bekalan yang dihadapi oleh banyak negara dan kejayaan memperoleh pelbagai jenis vaksin sekali mereka tersedia. A recent social media post claims that during the pandemic, individuals can request food and cash from convenience stores without being held legally responsible, citing Article 24 of the Criminal Code and suggesting that a necessity defense applies in emergencies. This post has generated significant interest and confusion, particularly as many people face economic hardships amid public health crises. This article examines the accuracy of these assertions and provides necessary legal and practical context.

First, it is important to clarify what Article 24 of the Criminal Code states. While the specific numbering of criminal code articles can vary by country, laws regarding the "necessity defense" generally exist in many legal systems. The necessity defense allows individuals to break the law if doing so is necessary to prevent a greater harm, and no legal alternative exists. However, this defense is subject to strict limitations and is evaluated on a case-by-case basis.

The social media post suggests that anyone can approach a convenience store during a pandemic, request food or cash, and escape liability based on the necessity defense. This interpretation is misleading. The necessity defense is not a blanket permission to take property without consequence. It is a legal argument used in court after an alleged crime has occurred. For example, if someone takes food without paying, they may still be charged with theft. During a trial, the defendant can argue that their actions were necessary to avoid starvation or serious harm. The court then considers several factors: whether the harm avoided was greater than the harm caused, whether all legal alternatives were exhausted, and whether the action was proportional to the need.

Moreover, necessity defenses are rarely successful for property crimes like theft, especially if there was an opportunity to seek help from social services, charities, or government programs. Courts generally require proof that the defendant faced an immediate and severe threat, such as imminent risk of serious injury or death, and that their actions were the only way to avert that harm. Simply being in a difficult situation, even during a pandemic, does not automatically justify taking food or cash from a business.

The pandemic has certainly increased economic hardship, and many governments and organizations have expanded aid programs to help those in need. People struggling to afford food or basic necessities are encouraged to seek assistance through these official channels rather than resorting to potentially unlawful actions. Convenience stores are typically private businesses, and employees may not have the authority or resources to provide food or cash on request.

In summary, the claim that anyone can legally demand food or cash from convenience stores during emergencies without liability is false. While the necessity defense exists in law, it is not a guarantee and is only applicable under very specific and urgent circumstances, subject to judicial scrutiny. Individuals should not assume immunity from prosecution based on emergency conditions alone. Seeking lawful assistance remains the recommended course of action during times of crisis.

Un post recent de pe rețelele sociale susține că, în timpul pandemiei, persoanele pot solicita mâncare sau bani de la magazine de conveniență fără a fi responsabilizate legal, citând articolul 24 al Codului Penal și sugerezând că se aplică apărarea necesității în situații de urgență. Acest post a generat interes și confuzie semnificativă, în special întrucât mulți oameni se confruntă cu dificultăți economice în timpul crizelor de sănătate publică. Articolul analizează exactitatea acestor afirmații și oferă context legal și practic necesar.

În primul rând, este important să se clarifice ce spune articolul 24 al Codului Penal. Deși numărul exact al articolului poate varia în funcție de țară, legile privind „apărarea necesității” există în general în multe sisteme juridice. Apărarea necesității permite persoanelor să încalce legea dacă acest lucru este necesar pentru a preveni un prejudiciu mai mare, iar nu există alte alternative legale. Totuși, această apărare este supusă limitări stricte și este evaluată pe cazuri individuale.

Postul de pe rețelele sociale sugerează că oricine poate apela la un magazin de conveniență în timpul pandemiei, să solicite mâncare sau bani și să evite responsabilitatea legală bazându-se pe apărarea necesității. Această interpretare este greșită. Apărarea necesității nu este o permisiune generală de a lua proprietate fără consecințe. Este un argument legal folosit în instanță după ce un criminal a fost presupus. De exemplu, dacă cineva ia mâncare fără a plăti, poate fi totuși acuzat de furt. În timpul procesului, acuzatul poate argumenta că acțiunile sale erau necesare pentru a evita foamea sau un prejudiciu grav. Curtea consideră apoi mai mulți factori: dacă prejudiciul evitat era mai mare decât prejudiciul cauzat, dacă toate alternativele legale au fost epuizate și dacă acțiunea era proporțională cu nevoia.

În plus, apărarea necesității este rar de succes pentru crime de proprietate, cum ar fi furtul, mai ales dacă a fost oportunitatea de a cere ajutor din partea serviciilor sociale, caritativă sau a programelor guvernamentale. Curțile cer în mod general dovezi că acuzatul a întâmpinat o amenințare imediată și gravă, cum ar fi un risc iminent de leziuni severe sau deces, și că acțiunile sale erau singura modalitate de a evita acest prejudiciu. Pur și simplu a fi într-o situație dificilă, chiar și în timpul pandemiei, nu justifică automat luarea mâncării sau a banilor dintr-o afacere.

Pandemia a crescut cu siguranță dificultățile economice, iar multe guverne și organizații au extins programele de asistență pentru a ajuta pe cei care au nevoie. Persoanele care își luptă cu cheltuielile pentru mâncare sau pentru nevoile de bază sunt încurajate să caute asistență prin aceste canale oficiale, mai degrabă decât să se expună potențial unor acțiuni ilegale. Magazinele de conveniență sunt de obicei afaceri private, iar angajații lor nu au autoritatea sau resursele necesare pentru a oferi mâncare sau bani la cerere.

În concluzie, afirmația conform căreia oricine poate cere legal mâncare sau bani din magazine de conveniență în timpul urgențelor fără a fi responsabilizat este falsă. Deși apărarea necesității există în lege, aceasta nu este o garanție și este aplicabilă doar în circumstanțe foarte specifice și urgente, sub supravegherea instanței. Persoanele nu ar trebui să presupună imunitate față de procesare doar pe baza condițiilor de urgență. Căutarea unui ajutor legal rămâne soluția recomandată în timpul crizelor.
